questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An elderly woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops marked hair loss. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced hair loss is typically classified as anagen effluvium. This occurs because chemotherapeutic agents target rapidly dividing cells, which include the hair matrix cells during their active growth (anagen) phase. The damage causes the hair shaft to narrow and eventually break or fall out suddenly and diffusely within weeks of starting treatment. Regarding the distractors, telogen effluvium (Option A) is a delayed shedding triggered by stress or illness that pushes hairs into the resting phase prematurely. Trichotillomania (Option B) is a behavioral disorder involving compulsive hair pulling resulting in irregular patches. Alopecia areata (Option D) is an autoimmune condition causing well-defined circular patches of hair loss. Because chemotherapy specifically interrupts the mitotic activity of the hair bulb during the growth cycle, anagen effluvium is the correct pathological diagnosis
questions.learning: Chemotherapy-induced hair loss is typically classified as anagen effluvium. This occurs because chemotherapeutic agents target rapidly dividing cells, which include the hair matrix cells during their active growth (anagen) phase.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man is reported deceased, and relatives state that he had a tattoo. However, no tattoo is visible on external examination during autopsy. To confirm its presence, further evaluation is required. What is the most appropriate site to examine to locate the tattoo?
questions.explanation: Tattooing involves injecting insoluble pigment granules into the dermal layer of the skin. Over time, macrophages and other immune cells phagocytose these pigment particles. Because these particles are often too large or chemically stable to be broken down, they are transported via the lymphatic system to the regional draining lymph nodes. In cases where a body is decomposed, charred, or if an attempt was made to surgically remove or chemically bleach a tattoo, the skin may no longer show visible ink. However, the pigment remains permanently sequestered within the regional lymph nodes, often staining them the same color as the original tattoo ink. This makes lymph node examination a vital forensic tool for identifying individuals with known tattoos when the skin is compromised. The spleen (Option A), liver (Option D), and arteries (Option B) are not part of the primary lymphatic drainage pathway for dermal pigments and would not reliably contain concentrated tattoo ink for identification purposes
questions.learning: Tattooing involves injecting insoluble pigment granules into the dermal layer of the skin. Over time, macrophages and other immune cells phagocytose these pigment particles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following measures are associated with an increased life span?
options: Moderate or regular exercise for 30 min
Pharmacological intervention with proton pump inhibitors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent

Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent will increase lifespan.

Caloric restriction reduces both the degree of oxidative damage and the associated decline in function. It decreases the steady-state concentrations of products of oxidative damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids. This is due to decreased production of mitochondrial superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide and increased antioxidant production. Overall, caloric restriction depresses the rate of energy metabolism.

Caloric restriction increases longevity both by reducing the signaling intensity of the insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) pathway and by increasing sirtuins (NAD-dependent protein deacetylases).

The attenuation of IGF-1 signaling leads to lower rates of cell growth and metabolism that reduces cellular damage. A similar effect is produced by rapamycin. An increase in sirtuins (particularly sirtuin-6) promotes the expression of several genes whose products increase longevity by activating DNA repair enzymes through deacylation.

Caloric restriction delays the onset of age-associated diseases such as cancer (including lymphomas and breast and prostate cancers), nephropathy, and cataracts. The onset of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and the development of autoimmune diseases is also decreased by caloric restriction.
questions.learning: Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent will increase lifespan. Caloric restriction reduces both the degree of oxidative damage and the associated decline in function.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding oligohydramnios: 1. It is defined on USG when maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than 5 cm. 2. It is defined on USG when AFI is less than 5 cm. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

Oligohydramnios refers to decreased amniotic fluid volume and is associated with increased maternal and fetal morbidity. It is diagnosed by ultrasonography using either the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) or the Single Deepest Vertical Pocket (SDVP/Maximum Vertical Pocket, MVP).

Why is B correct?

• 1. It is defined on USG when maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than 5 cm. ✗

• Oligohydramnios is defined when the Single Deepest Vertical Pocket (SDVP/MVP) is <2 cm, not <5 cm.

• 2. It is defined on USG when AFI is less than 5 cm. ✓

• AFI <5 cm is the standard ultrasound definition of oligohydramnios.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. Neurological examination reveals positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. The diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis is suspected. Which of the following medications is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin

This presentation is classic for meningococcal meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash).

Close contacts are at high risk due to nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis.

Rifampicin is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis, as it eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage.

| Drug | Role in Meningococcal Prophylaxis

| ---- | ---------------------------------

| Rifampicin | First-line

| Ciprofloxacin | Alternative

| Ceftriaxone | Alternative

| Others | ❌ Not used
questions.learning: Rifampicin — This presentation is classic for meningococcal meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash). Close contacts are at high risk due to nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the cycles listed below is absent in muscle tissue?
questions.explanation: Ketogenesis, the metabolic process of producing ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA, occurs exclusively in the mitochondria of liver cells. While muscle tissue can utilize ketone bodies for energy during starvation, it lacks the necessary enzymatic machinery to synthesize them. Glycogenolysis (Option A) and glycogenesis (Option C) are both highly active in muscle tissue, where glycogen serves as a critical local energy reserve for contraction. Lipolysis (Option D), the breakdown of triacylglycerols, also occurs in muscle cells to provide fatty acids for beta-oxidation during aerobic exercise. Because the liver is the sole organ capable of significant ketone body production to be exported to other tissues like the brain and muscles, ketogenesis is definitively absent from muscle tissue. This metabolic compartmentalization ensures that the liver remains the primary provider of alternative fuels during periods of low glucose availability
questions.learning: Ketogenesis, the metabolic process of producing ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA, occurs exclusively in the mitochondria of liver cells. While muscle tissue can utilize ketone bodies for energy during starvation, it lacks the necessary enzymatic machinery to…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A tympanometry tracing shows a shallow peak occurring at a pressure of 0 daPa, as indicated by the arrow. Based on this tympanometric finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The tympanogram features a shallow peak at normal middle ear pressure (0 daPa), which is diagnostic of a Type As pattern. This indicates a state of reduced compliance or stiffening of the tympano-ossicular system. Common clinical causes include otosclerosis (stapes fixation), tympanosclerosis, or a thickened tympanic membrane. Type A (Option A) has a normal peak height reflecting normal middle ear function. Type B (Option B) is a flat tracing indicating middle ear fluid or a perforation. Type Ad (Option D) shows an extremely high peak (hypercompliance), typically associated with ossicular discontinuity or a very thin tympanic membrane. Because the peak is centered at the correct pressure but is pathologically shallow, Type As is the correct classification for this stiffened system
questions.learning: The tympanogram features a shallow peak at normal middle ear pressure (0 daPa), which is diagnostic of a Type As pattern. This indicates a state of reduced compliance or stiffening of the tympano-ossicular system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What test is used to check for freeze damage to vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shake test

The freeze damage to vaccines is detected by Shake test.

• A frozen vaccine is used as a control vial and the vial suspected to be damaged by freezing is taken as the test vial.
• Both are shaken after thawing and the rate of sedimentation is compared.
• If the rate of sedimentation in test vial is slower than the control vial, then it is usable and has not been damaged.
• Some of the most widely used vaccines are freeze-sensitive. Examples: Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis, Liquid Haemophilus influenza type b (Hib), Hepatitis B.
questions.learning: Shake test — The freeze damage to vaccines is detected by Shake test. • A frozen vaccine is used as a control vial and the vial suspected to be damaged by freezing is taken as the test vial. • Both are shaken after thawing and the rate of sedimentation is…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Just after delivery, the position of the uterus corresponds to the level of how many weeks?
questions.explanation: Immediately after delivery of the baby (and placenta), the uterus undergoes rapid contraction and retraction. At this stage, the uterine fundus is palpable at the level of the umbilicus, which corresponds approximately to the size of a 20-week pregnant uterus. During pregnancy, the uterus gradually enlarges: 1. At 12 weeks → just above the symphysis pubis 2. At 20 weeks → at the level of the umbilicus 3. At 28 weeks → above the umbilicus After delivery, although the fetus and placenta are expelled, the uterus does not immediately return to its pre-pregnant size. Instead, it remains enlarged and firm to prevent hemorrhage. This postpartum uterine size corresponds to about 20 weeks gestation, and then it gradually involutes over the next few weeks. Why other options are wrong: (B) 16 weeks → Below umbilicus (C) 12 weeks → Too small; uterus already involutes later (D) 28 weeks → Too large; corresponds to late pregnancy
questions.learning: Immediately after delivery of the baby (and placenta), the uterus undergoes rapid contraction and retraction. At this stage, the uterine fundus is palpable at the level of the umbilicus, which corresponds approximately to the size of a 20-week pregnant uterus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Macrophages play an important role in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation. Which of the following cells perform the same function in the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages located in the liver that form part of the mononuclear phagocyte system. These are present, lining the walls of the sinusoids, not the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse).

Macrophages can be divided into:

* Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.

* Tissue macrophages survive for months.

2 main functions of macrophages:

* Phagocytosis.

* Antigen presentation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Device shown in the image is used for which purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prevent transfusion related reactions

The image shows a leukoreduction filter which is used for filtering out donor WBCs. This helps in reducing the incidence of transfusion-related reactions by removing WBC microaggregates. The optimum time for performing leukoreduction is before the storage of blood.

Potential benefits include reduced risk of:

• Sensitization to HLA antigens (important for transplant patients & preventing platelet refractoriness)
• Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTR)
• CMV transmission

Note: CMV also has an affinity for monocytes and macrophages (types of WBCs). Reduction in WBCs is the cause for the decrease in CMV transmission (accidental benefit), and thus, the main purpose of a leukoreduction filter is not the prevention of CMV transmission (options A and C).

Possible reduced risk of:

• Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA- GVHD)
• Transfusion-related immuno-modulatory (TRIM) effects
• Transmitting variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease

Other Methods of Leucodepletion are:

• Specific leucodepletion filters (Most Efficient)
• Washing
• Freezing
• Buffy coat removal
• Micro-aggregate filtration
• Low leucocyte apheresis devices
questions.learning: Prevent transfusion related reactions — The image shows a leukoreduction filter which is used for filtering out donor WBCs. This helps in reducing the incidence of transfusion-related reactions by removing WBC microaggregates.

questions.text: L & H type Reed-Sternberg (RS) cell is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lymphocyte predominant

L & H type Reed–Sternberg cell is seen in lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.

It is characterized by the presence of lymphohistiocytic (L&H) variant RS cells that have a delicate multilobed, puffy nucleus resembling popped corn (popcorn cell). Other reactive cells, such as eosinophils, are scanty or absent, and typical RS cells are rare.

Unlike the RS variants in classical Hodgkin lymphoma, L&H variants express B cell markers (e.g., CD20) and usually fail to express CD15 and CD30.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman came to the hospital with complaints of excruciating paroxysmal pain on the right side of her lips, gums, and cheek. The episodes last for 2-3 min. Which of the following is incorrect regarding the primary drug used in the treatment of this condition?
options: It is a Chloride channel opener
It also has anti-epileptic activity against focal seizures
It can lead to hyponatremia in the elderly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is a Chloride channel opener

Severe, brief, unilateral facial pain involving lips, gums, and cheek is classic for trigeminal neuralgia.

Drug of choice: Carbamazepine

Mechanism of action:

• Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels → stabilizes hyperexcitable neuronal membranes
• Not a chloride channel opener (that allows Cl⁻ influx via GABA-A drugs)

Important adverse effects of carbamazepine:

• Agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia
• Hyponatremia (SIADH), especially in elderly
• Hepatotoxicity
• Also effective for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the value of normal tissue oncotic pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12 mmHg

The value of normal tissue oncotic pressure is 12 mmHg. It refers to the interstitial osmotic pressure.

The interstitial oncotic pressure, while very small, is the pressure exerted by a small amount of protein present in the interstitium that tends to pull fluids out of the capillaries. It is different for each organ based on the level of protein components. It is mostly negligible, but sometimes can be as high as 6 mmHg in the brain. The values are also positive in the liver and kidneys.

The colloid osmotic pressure or oncotic pressure is the osmotic pressure exerted due to the presence of colloidal proteins like albumin and globulin within the plasma. The colloidal proteins are impermeable to the semi-permeable cell membrane and cannot cross the membrane. Thus, it exerts osmotic pressure, which pulls fluid into the capillaries.

The lowest number in the given options is 12 mmHg and, hence, is the best possible answer to this question.
questions.learning: 12 mmHg The value of normal tissue oncotic pressure is 12 mmHg. It refers to the interstitial osmotic pressure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with long-standing Ménière’s disease suddenly collapses to the ground without loss of consciousness and without warning vertigo. He is able to get up immediately after the fall. What is the most likely explanation for this episode?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tumarkin otolithic crisis

•

Tumarkin otolithic crisis (drop attack) is a complication of long-standing Ménière’s disease characterized by sudden falls without warning, vertigo, or loss of consciousness, with immediate recovery.

•

Sudden stimulation or dysfunction of the otolithic organs (utricle/saccule) due to endolymphatic hydrops → abrupt loss of postural control → patient suddenly collapses.

Differentiation:

• Vertebrobasilar insufficiency → LOC or neurological deficits
• Tulio phenomenon → vertigo induced by loud sound
• Lermoyez syndrome → hearing improves after vertigo

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A breastfeeding mother complains of cramp- like pain in her breasts during nursing. Which hormone is mainly responsible for producing these sensations?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the hormone responsible for the "milk ejection reflex" (milk let-down) during breastfeeding. In response to the infant's suckling, oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary gland. It causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli of the breast, forcing milk into the ducts. These muscular contractions are what the mother perceives as "breast cramps." Additionally, oxytocin release during breastfeeding stimulates uterine contractions (postpartum "afterpains"), which helps with uterine involution. Progesterone (Option A) and Estrogen (Option B) are involved in breast development during pregnancy but their levels drop sharply after delivery to allow lactation. Prolactin (Option C), released from the anterior pituitary, is the hormone responsible for "milk production" (lactogenesis) rather than the physical ejection and associated cramping. Understanding this neuroendocrine reflex is vital for counseling nursing mothers on the physical sensations of breastfeeding and the physiological benefits of early and frequent feeding for maternal recovery
questions.learning: Oxytocin is the hormone responsible for the "milk ejection reflex" (milk let-down) during breastfeeding. In response to the infant's suckling, oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary gland.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a distorted or irregularly shaped eye following delayed healing of a corneal ulcer, despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. Based on the clinical features and examination findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anterior staphyloma is a condition characterized by a bulging, ectatic scar of the cornea that is lined internally by uveal tissue (iris). It typically occurs as a late complication of a perforated corneal ulcer. When an ulcer heals with a thin, weak scar (pseudocornea), the intraocular pressure causes this weak area to protrude outward. The "deformed" and "dark" appearance mentioned comes from the iris pigment visible through the thin scar tissue. Option A (Megalocornea) is a non-progressive congenital enlargement of a clear cornea. Option B (Conjunctivitis) is a superficial inflammation and would not cause eye deformity. Option C (Buphthalmos) is an enlargement of the entire globe due to congenital glaucoma in neonates. Treatment for a large anterior staphyloma is often cosmetic (staphylomectomy or enucleation), as the eye is typically blind. This case emphasizes the importance of managing corneal ulcers aggressively to prevent perforation
questions.learning: Anterior staphyloma is a condition characterized by a bulging, ectatic scar of the cornea that is lined internally by uveal tissue (iris). It typically occurs as a late complication of a perforated corneal ulcer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In given image, nucleus of marked nerve is related to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cervical spinal segment

The correct answer is Cervical spinal segment.

The marked nerve is the phrenic nerve, whose motor nucleus lies in the ventral horn of cervical spinal cord segments C3–C5.

It provides the sole motor supply to the diaphragm, with the mnemonic “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.”

Midbrain, pons, and medulla contain cranial nerve nuclei, not the origin of the phrenic nerve.
questions.learning: Cervical spinal segment — The correct answer is Cervical spinal segment. The marked nerve is the phrenic nerve, whose motor nucleus lies in the ventral horn of cervical spinal cord segments C3–C5.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with generalized abdominal pain. He has a history of prolonged NSAID use. On examination, abdominal rigidity is noted. An abdominal X-ray shows significant findings related to his condition. Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with acute generalized abdominal pain and abdominal rigidity, which suggests peritonitis. A key clue is the history of long-term NSAID use, a major risk factor for peptic ulcer formation and subsequent perforation. The X-ray (erect chest/abdominal film) typically shows free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum), which is a classic sign of hollow viscus perforation, most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Intestinal obstruction : Shows multiple air-fluid levels and dilated bowel loops, not free air under diaphragm or rigidity. (B) Pericarditis : Presents with chest pain and ECG changes, not abdominal rigidity or pneumoperitoneum. (D) Gallstones : Cause right upper quadrant pain, not generalized rigidity or free air on X-ray
questions.learning: The patient presents with acute generalized abdominal pain and abdominal rigidity, which suggests peritonitis. A key clue is the history of long-term NSAID use, a major risk factor for peptic ulcer formation and subsequent perforation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not reversed with the administration of atropine?
options: Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and it effectively counteracts parasympathetic overstimulation at smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and exocrine glands. Therefore, it is useful in conditions such as bradycardia (Option A), excessive salivation (Option C), and bronchoconstriction (Option D), which are mediated by M₂ and M₃ muscarinic receptors. However, muscle weakness caused by neuromuscular blocking agents is mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Nm) located at the neuromuscular junction. Atropine has no action on nicotinic receptors, and thus cannot reverse skeletal muscle paralysis or weakness. Reversal of neuromuscular blockade requires an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine, which increases acetylcholine levels at the neuromuscular junction to competitively overcome the blockade. Atropine is administered concurrently with neostigmine only to prevent muscarinic side effects (such as bradycardia, bronchospasm, and salivation) caused by increased acetylcholine. Therefore, atropine cannot directly improve skeletal muscle strength, as it does not act on the receptors responsible for neuromuscular transmission
questions.learning: Atropine is a competitive antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and it effectively counteracts parasympathetic overstimulation at smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and exocrine glands.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: When a family member volunteers to donate blood for a patient injured in a road traffic accident, which of the following tests is not routinely required before proceeding with the blood transfusion?
questions.explanation: To ensure the safety of the blood supply, all donated blood must undergo rigorous mandatory screening for major transfusion-transmitted infections. Standard screening protocols include testing for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (Option B), Hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies (Option C), and HIV types 1 and 2 antibodies or p24 antigen (Option D). Additionally, screening for syphilis and malaria is typically required. Hepatitis A (Option A) is NOT typically tested in routine pre-transfusion protocols. The Hepatitis A virus is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, has a very short-lived viremic phase, and does not cause a chronic carrier state. Because the risk of transmission through blood products is negligible compared to the chronic, blood-borne nature of HBV, HCV, and HIV, it is not a part of mandatory blood safety testing. Thus, Hepatitis A is the correct "except" choice for routine donor screening

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia is the type of visual loss seen when the lesion is located at which one of the following anatomical locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Temporal lobe

A lesion involving the temporal lobe, specifically the Meyer’s loop (inferior optic radiations), produces a contralateral homonymous superior (upper) quadrantanopia, classically described as “pie in the sky” visual field defect.

The inferior retinal fibers, which carry information from the superior visual field, pass anteriorly through the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) before reaching the occipital cortex. Damage to these fibers results in loss of the contralateral upper visual field in both eyes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Frontal lobe: Does not contain the visual pathway responsible for quadrantanopia.
• C. Parietal lobe: Contains the superior optic radiations, and lesions produce contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia (“pie on the floor”).
• D. Occipital lobe: Lesions usually cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing if due to posterior cerebral artery infarction.
questions.learning: Temporal lobe — A lesion involving the temporal lobe, specifically the Meyer’s loop (inferior optic radiations), produces a contralateral homonymous superior (upper) quadrantanopia, classically described as “pie in the sky” visual field defect.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged housewife consumed rodenticide powder and presented with K+ levels of 2.5meq. On examination, irregular pulse with muscle paralysis is present. ECG shows ventricular ectopics. What is the suspected poison?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Barium carbonate

The above clinical scenario with a presentation of hypokalemia, cardiac arrhythmia and paralysis after consumption of rodenticide poison is caused by Barium carbonate.

Barium carbonate is used in rat poised, a local corrosive irritant that, after absorption, mainly acts on muscles including the heart muscles.

The initial symptoms manifest as intense gastrointestinal distress, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Subsequently, muscle cramps and stiffness, pupil dilation, tongue and larynx paralysis, and vertigo occur. Early impacts on the heart lead to elevated blood pressure, a slow and irregular pulse, and potential cardiac arrest in systole. Among the most notable changes are a loss of reflexes and paralysis.

Treatment involves the following steps:

1. Gastric lavage to remove contents and administration of either sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate solution to precipitate barium as insoluble sulfate.
2. Intravenous administration of 10 ml of 10% sodium sulfate every 15 minutes to convert the soluble salt into insoluble sulfate.
3. Purging with magnesium sulfate and repeated bowel lavage.
4. Symptomatic management.

Other options:

Option A: Aluminium phosphide (ALP) is a solid fumigant pesticide, insecticide and rodenticide. ALP has a garlicky odour. Phosphine is a toxic agent. It acts by inhibiting the electron transport resulting from preferential inhibition of cytochrome oxidase.Severe toxicity produces ARDS, cardiac arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, pulmonary oedema, convulsions and coma. Cardiogenic shock is the most common cause of death, associated with higher mortality(35%- 100%) but does not cause hypokalaemia.

Option B: Zinc phosphide poisoning can cause symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and weakness. However, these symptoms are generally less severe compared to aluminium phosphide poisoning due to the highly toxic nature of phosphine gas released by aluminium phosphide.

Option D: Warfarin is an anticoagulant used in rat poison but is not directly associated with hypokalemia.
questions.learning: Barium carbonate — The above clinical scenario with a presentation of hypokalemia, cardiac arrhythmia and paralysis after consumption of rodenticide poison is caused by Barium carbonate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging swelling near the wrist joint over the past three months. Based on the X-ray findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays an expansile, multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance. The lesion extends right up to the subchondral bone (articular surface). These are pathognomonic radiological features of Osteoclastoma, also known as a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) (Option C). GCT is typically seen in young adults (ages 20–40) and is locally aggressive. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) presents with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Osteosarcoma (Option B) would show a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and a Codman’s triangle. Osteochondroma (Option D) appears as a bony outgrowth on a stalk (exostosis). Therefore, the subarticular location and soap-bubble morphology confirm Osteoclastoma as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The X-ray displays an expansile, multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the inhalational anaesthetic agent used for induction in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sevoflurane

Sevoflurane is the inhalational anaesthetic agent used for induction in children. (Option C)

It is the preferred agent due to its non-pungent sweet-smelling nature and rapid increase in alveolar concentration on administration. Its low blood solubility helps during emergence from the effects of anaesthesia, reducing the post-operative delay in the patient's recovery from anaesthesia.

Desflurane and isoflurane are avoided for inhalation induction because they are pungent and associated with coughing, breath-holding and laryngospasm. They are usually used for the maintenance of anaesthesia. Desflurane is preferred in patients with renal and liver disease and isoflurane is preferred in neurosurgery and cardiac surgery.

Due to its second-gas effect, nitrous oxide is mainly used as a carrier gas for other inhalational agents and not given alone.
questions.learning: Sevoflurane Sevoflurane is the inhalational anaesthetic agent used for induction in children. (Option C) It is the preferred agent due to its non-pungent sweet-smelling nature and rapid increase in alveolar concentration on administration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a head injury. The CT scan is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epidural hematoma

An epidural hematoma (EDH) is an arterial hemorrhage that occurs between the inner table of the skull and the periosteal layer of the dura mater, most commonly due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone (pterion) fracture. On CT scan, it appears as a hyperdense, biconvex (lentiform), extra-axial collection that is limited by cranial sutures because the dura is firmly attached at suture lines.

Why not the other options?

• B. Subdural hematoma: Caused by rupture of bridging veins. CT shows a crescent-shaped (concave) extra-axial collection that crosses sutures but is limited by the falx and tentorium.
• C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Blood is seen within the basal cisterns and cerebral sulci, producing a “star sign” on CT rather than a localized biconvex collection.
• D. Intracerebral hemorrhage: Appears as a hyperdense intraparenchymal lesion within the brain tissue, not as an extra-axial collection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is best method to survey the injection practices of health workers?
options: Direct observation with a structured checklist
In-depth interview with the healthcare provider
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct observation with a structured checklist

Direct observation with a structured checklist is the best method to survey the injection practices of health workers.

Checklist of practices for assessment or evaluation include:-

• In order not to harm the patient, each procedure should be administered with a new sterile single-use device, using the right medication, vaccine or fluid for infusion.
• In order not to expose the provider to any avoidable risk, in general, any needles used during a procedure should be placed in a puncture-proof closed container immediately after use without recapping. In addition, providers of these procedures should be fully vaccinated against Hepatitis-B.
•  In order that any waste produced during the performance of a procedure does not become a hazard for other people, used sharps waste and infectious non-sharps waste should be safely managed.
questions.learning: Direct observation with a structured checklist Direct observation with a structured checklist is the best method to survey the injection practices of health workers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following functions is not carried out by the intestinal epithelium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bile salt secretion

Bile salts are not secreted by the intestinal epithelium. They are secreted by the liver.

The intestinal epithelium has multiple roles to be performed in the functioning of the gastrointestinal system.

* Absorptive function: provides surface area and mechanisms for absorption of digestive products

* Secretory function: intestinal digestive enzyme secretion

* Protective function: both formation of the physical barrier and chemical barrier via the production of mucous

Bile salts are secreted by the liver from cholesterol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones primarily acts on the post-ovulatory endometrium?
questions.explanation: Following ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes high levels of Progesterone. Progesterone is the primary hormone that acts on the post-ovulatory endometrium, transforming it into a secretory state that is receptive to embryo implantation. While Estrogen (Option D) is present throughout the cycle and helps maintain the lining, it is the dominant hormone of the pre-ovulatory (proliferative) phase. Luteinizing hormone (Option A) and Follicular stimulating hormone (Option B) are pituitary gonadotropins that stimulate the ovaries but do not directly act on the endometrial tissue to induce secretory changes. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses, leading to a sharp drop in progesterone, which triggers the shedding of the endometrium during menstruation. Understanding this hormonal sequence is fundamental for evaluating menstrual irregularities and infertility. The secretory transformation of the endometrium is the defining biological event of the luteal phase

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with hypoxemia and a normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. What can be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoventilation

All of the given options can cause hypoxemia out of which the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) remains normal in hypoventilation.

The A-a gradient or the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient refers to the difference between the oxygen concentration in the alveoli (PAO2) and oxygen concentration in the arterial system (PaO2).

A-a gradient= PAO2 - PaO2

In hypoventilation, patients lack oxygen tension in the respiratory system as well as their arterial system. This results in a decrease in both PAO2 and PaO2 and A-a gradient remains normal. Hypoventilation can be seen in CNS depression, neuromuscular diseases such as myasthenia gravis, kyphoscoliosis, vertebral fractures, etc.

Other options:

Option A- In a right-to-left shunt, a portion of the pulmonary blood flow gets shunted away from the alveoli. This results in ventilation without perfusion which causes a higher V/Q ratio. Here, diffusion between capillaries and alveoli is unaffected,  but the arterial PaO2 is decreased due to the lack of oxygenation of the shunted blood. This results in hypoxemia and an increased A-a gradient. In the cases of the shunt, oxygenation does not improve hypoxemia.

Option B- Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia.

Low V/Q mismatch occurs in chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD), asthma, interstitial lung disease, etc. In these cases, the A-a oxygen gradient is increased due to a defect in diffusion resulting in hypoxemia.

A high V/Q ratio is seen in pulmonary embolism (PE) where there is wasted ventilation. The alveolar oxygen is normal but there is decreased perfusion resulting in increased A-a gradient.

Inspiratory hypoxia, seen at high altitudes, can cause a V/Q mismatch. The decreased atmospheric pressure causes a decreased PAO2. There is normal diffusion which suggests a normal A-a gradient while the arterial PaO2 decreases, leading to hypoxemia.

Hypoventilation is the better answer as the cause of the V/Q mismatch is not specified.

Option D: Alveolar membrane damage affects diffusion between the alveoli and capillaries. The oxygen levels in the arterial blood decrease even though alveoli are being ventilated. This leads to an increased A-a gradient.
questions.learning: Hypoventilation All of the given options can cause hypoxemia out of which the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) remains normal in hypoventilation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Match the following genetic disorders with their inheritance patterns:

A. Cystic fibrosis
1. Autosomal dominant

B. Leber optic neuropathy
2. Autosomal recessive

C. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
3. X-Linked recesssive

D. Myotonic dystrophy
4. Mitochondrial
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A2, B4, C3, D1

Genetic disorder
Inheritance pattern

A. Cystic fibrosis
Autosomal recessive

B. Leber optic neuropathy
Mitochondrial

C. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
X-linked recessive

D. Myotonic dystrophy
Autosomal dominant

Cystic fibrosis: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder; both parents must carry a copy of the mutated gene in order for the child to be affected.

Leber optic neuropathy: Leber optic neuropathy is a mitochondrial genetic disorder. This means that the mutated gene is located on the mitochondrial DNA, which is DNA that is outside of the nucleus of the cell. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited solely from the mother.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive genetic disorder. This means that the mutated gene is located on the X chromosome. Males have only one X chromosome, so if they inherit a mutated copy of the gene, they will be affected. Females have two X chromosomes, so if they inherit one mutated copy of the gene, they will be carriers.

Myotonic dystrophy: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder. This means that only one parent needs to carry a copy of the mutated gene in order for their child to be affected.
questions.learning: A2, B4, C3, D1 Genetic disorder Inheritance pattern A. Cystic fibrosis Autosomal recessive B.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes simplex

Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in herpes simplex infection.

The classic Cowdry type A (Lipshutz) inclusion appears as a light purple, homogeneous intranuclear structure surrounded by a clear halo. The inclusions stain with antibodies to HSV, permitting a rapid, specific diagnosis of HSV infection.
questions.learning: Herpes simplex Cowdry type — A inclusions are seen in herpes simplex infection. The classic Cowdry type A (Lipshutz) inclusion appears as a light purple, homogeneous intranuclear structure surrounded by a clear halo.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with lethargy, vomiting, and poor feeding following a period of prolonged fasting. Laboratory evaluation shows hypoglycemia with low ketone levels and mild hepatomegaly, suggesting a disorder of fat metabolism. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease)
questions.explanation: This presentation is the classic clinical hallmark of MCAD deficiency, the most common fatty acid beta-oxidation defect. Normally, during fasting, the body switches to fat oxidation to produce energy and ketones. In MCAD deficiency, the inability to break down medium-chain fats leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and fat accumulation in the liver (mild hepatomegaly). Her's disease (Option A) causes fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, but ketone production remains normal because fat oxidation is intact. Hereditary fructose intolerance (Option C) occurs after fructose ingestion, not fasting. Von Gierke disease (Option D) presents with severe hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, but ketones are typically normal or even high rather than low. Thus, the specific failure to produce ketones during a hypoglycemic fasting state identifies MCAD deficiency
questions.learning: This presentation is the classic clinical hallmark of MCAD deficiency, the most common fatty acid beta-oxidation defect. Normally, during fasting, the body switches to fat oxidation to produce energy and ketones.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with acute worsening of dyspnea. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.24, pCO₂ 60 mmHg, pO₂ 52 mmHg, and HCO₃ [value not provided]. What is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?
questions.explanation: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). The patient is in acute respiratory failure due to a COPD exacerbation. His ABG shows respiratory acidosis (pH 7.24, 60 mmHg) and hypoxemia ( 52 mmHg). For a COPD patient who is acidotic but still awake/stable, Non-invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV) (Option C) is the gold-standard first-line treatment. NIPPV reduces the work of breathing, improves gas exchange, and significantly lowers the need for invasive ventilation and hospital mortality. Endotracheal intubation (Option A) and invasive ventilation (Option B) are reserved for those who fail NIPPV or present in coma/arrest. Lung volume reduction surgery (Option D) is a chronic management option for end-stage emphysema, not for acute failure. Therefore, because NIPPV is highly effective at reversing the acidosis while avoiding the complications of an artificial airway, it is the definitive most appropriate choice. Clinicians must monitor the patient closely for improvement within the first few hours. .
questions.learning: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). The patient is in acute respiratory failure due to a COPD exacerbation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents with restricted abduction and internal rotation of the hip. The X-ray image shown below demonstrates characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: (SCFE). SCFE is an orthopedic emergency that classically occurs in overweight or rapidly growing adolescents (ages 10–16). It involves the displacement of the femoral neck from the capital femoral epiphysis through the growth plate. The clinical presentation—restricted internal rotation and abduction in a 13-year-old—is the hallmark of this condition. The provided X-ray demonstrates the pathognomonic "ice cream falling off a cone" sign, where the femoral head is slipped posteriorly and inferiorly. Perthes Disease (Option B) usually affects younger children (ages 4–8) and shows a fragmented femoral head. DDH (Option C) is an infant condition. Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option D) involves spinal fusion and sacroiliitis, typically presenting later in life with chronic back pain. SCFE requires immediate non-weight bearing and surgical fixation (pinning) to prevent avascular necrosis. Thus, SCFE is the diagnosis
questions.learning: SCFE is an orthopedic emergency that classically occurs in overweight or rapidly growing adolescents (ages 10–16). It involves the displacement of the femoral neck from the capital femoral epiphysis through the growth plate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about of proteoglycans?
options: Made of amino acids and sugars
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Holds less water

Proteoglycans can hold large amounts of water, and not less.

Proteoglycans are made of a central protein core with O-linked glycosaminoglycan side-chains. They hold large quantities of water and occupy space.

They provide the ground substance of connective tissue.

Chondroitin sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan that is bound to a protein to form chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan. It is present in the extracellular matrix. Hyaluronic acid and heparin are examples of glycosaminoglycans.

All of the other statements regarding proteoglycans are true.
questions.learning: Holds less water Proteoglycans can hold large amounts of water, and not less. Proteoglycans are made of a central protein core with O-linked glycosaminoglycan side-chains.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent infections arising from the lesion depicted in the image. Based on the clinical features and appearance of this lesion, which of the following statements regarding it is correct?
options: Derived from ectoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from the pouch of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from mesoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from ectoderm of 3rd and 4th arch
questions.explanation: The clinical image depicts a preauricular sinus, a common congenital malformation. Developmentally, the external ear (pinna) is formed by the fusion of six auricular hillocks (of His) derived from the ectoderm of the first (Mandibular) and second (Hyoid) pharyngeal arches. A preauricular sinus results from the incomplete fusion of these hillocks, specifically between the first and second arches. Because it originates from the skin-forming layer, it is an ectodermal derivative lined with squamous epithelium. Pharyngeal pouches (Option B) are endodermal and give rise to structures like the Eustachian tube and tonsils. Mesodermal derivatives (Option C) include the cartilages and muscles of the arches. The third and fourth arches (Option D) contribute to the lower neck and laryngeal structures. These sinuses often remain asymptomatic unless they become infected, requiring antibiotics or surgical excision. They are frequently found anterior to the helix or the tragus

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is suggested in a young boy presenting with a fissured tongue, cracked lips, lesions at the angles of the mouth, and reduced red blood cell glutathione reductase activity on investigation?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of glossitis (fissured tongue), cheilosis (fissured lips), and angular stomatitis (lesions at the corners of the mouth) is highly suggestive of Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency. The biochemical hallmark of this deficiency is decreased erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, as flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), a derivative of B2, is an essential cofactor for this enzyme. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option A) leads to megaloblastic anemia and neurological issues. Vitamin B3 deficiency (Option B) causes pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds" (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Biotin deficiency (Option C) typically presents with dermatitis and hair loss. Because the biochemical test mentioned is the specific gold standard for assessing riboflavin status, Riboflavin is the definitive diagnosis. Early identification is crucial, as these mucocutaneous symptoms are reversible with oral supplementation
questions.learning: The clinical triad of glossitis (fissured tongue), cheilosis (fissured lips), and angular stomatitis (lesions at the corners of the mouth) is highly suggestive of Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn at birth was noticed to have a herniated liver and small intestine via the umbilicus. The herniated mass was covered with membranes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Omphalocele

A newborn with a herniated liver and small intestine via the umbilicus and the herniated mass being covered with membranes are both indicative of an omphalocele.

Failure of the intestinal loops to return to the abdominal cavity results in omphalocele or exomphalos which is covered with a membrane.

Omphalocele is a congenital malformation in which the abdominal viscera protrudes through a wide umbilical defect. The defect arises due to failure of the intestinal loops in the physiological umbilical hernia to return to the body cavity during the 6th to 10th weeks. The bowel loops are covered by amnion.

A small omphalocele contains only the intestines. A large omphalocele may contain other viscera such as stomach, liver, spleen, and large intestine, along with the small intestine. Omphalocele is commonly associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., trisomy 13, trisomy 18, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome) and causes increased levels of α-fetoprotein.

Other options:

Option B: Gastroschisis should be ruled out while evaluating an omphalocele. Unlike an omphalocele, it lacks a covering membranous sac. It is typically found in a paraumbilical position, most often to the right of the umbilicus.

Option C: In a persistent vitellointestinal duct, the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length. This results in the formation of direct communication between the umbilicus and the intestinal tract. A fecal discharge may then be found at the umbilicus.

Option D: Bochdalek hernia (posterior) is the most common type of diaphragmatic hernia. Herniation occurs through the pleuroperitoneal foramen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A lady cleans her cat litter regularly to avoid infection by toxoplasma during her pregnancy. What is the infective stage of this organism in the cat feces?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oocysts

The infective stage of Toxoplasma found in the cat feces is oocysts.

The oocysts develop from the sexual reproduction of Toxoplasma in the gut lumen of the cat and pass out via the feces. It takes 1 to 5 days for the oocysts to become infective after being excreted in the feces. Hence, daily removal of cat litter and safe disposal can prevent infection.

Both asexual reproduction (schizogony) and sexual reproduction (gametogony) occur within definitive hosts such as cats. The tachyzoites and tissue cysts represent stages in asexual multiplication, while the oocyst is formed by sexual reproduction, which occurs only in the definitive hosts such as cats.

Only the asexual forms i.e., tachyzoites, and tissue cysts are present in intermediate hosts such as humans, mice, rats, etc.

Humans acquire the infection upon consumption of meat containing tissue cysts, food or water containing mature oocysts, or fingers contaminated by cat feces.

Manifestations are mostly asymptomatic and if symptomatic can be congenital or acquired. Features such as fever, headache, myalgia, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy commonly affect the cervical lymph nodes.

Central nervous system involvement is observed in toxoplasma infection affecting immunocompromised individuals. Toxoplasma infection in pregnancy can lead to congenital toxoplasmosis that most frequently presents with chorioretinitis.
questions.learning: Oocysts — The infective stage of Toxoplasma found in the cat feces is oocysts. The oocysts develop from the sexual reproduction of Toxoplasma in the gut lumen of the cat and pass out via the feces.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with iron- deficiency anemia, painful and tender joints, and bleeding tendencies. Her diet largely consists of packaged and reheated foods. Based on her dietary habits and clinical features, which antioxidant deficiency is most likely responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s clinical presentation of bleeding manifestations (such as petechiae or bruising) and painful, tender joints (hemarthrosis), combined with a diet lacking fresh produce (packaged/reheated meals), is pathognomonic for Scurvy. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a vital antioxidant and a necessary cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, an enzyme essential for stable collagen synthesis. Furthermore, Vitamin C enhances the absorption of dietary iron, explaining the concurrent iron-deficiency anemia. Glutathione (Option A) and beta-carotene (Option B) are important antioxidants but their deficiency does not cause this specific bleeding and joint syndrome. Zinc (Option D) deficiency leads to skin lesions and impaired wound healing but not systemic bleeding manifestations. Because Vitamin C is heat-labile and easily destroyed by cooking/reheating, the patient’s dietary habits directly support this specific nutritional deficiency as the underlying cause
questions.learning: The patient’s clinical presentation of bleeding manifestations (such as petechiae or bruising) and painful, tender joints (hemarthrosis), combined with a diet lacking fresh produce (packaged/reheated meals), is pathognomonic for Scurvy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent abdominal pain and a history of blood in stools. On examination, there are dark pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

Classic Triad of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

1. Hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine (especially jejunum)

2. Mucocutaneous pigmentation

• Dark spots on lips
• Oral mucosa
• Perioral skin

3. Adolescent onset with GI bleeding or abdominal pain

These findings together are diagnostic of PJS.

The hamartomatous polyps can cause:

• GI bleeding
• Recurrent abdominal pain
• Intussusception (very common complication in PJS)

The pigmentation occurs due to melanin deposition in mucocutaneous areas.

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is caused by mutation in the: STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene

Inheritance pattern: Autosomal dominant.

A) Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)

• Caused by APC gene mutation
• Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps
• No mucocutaneous pigmentation

C) Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome

• Hamartomatous polyps but mainly in colon
• No characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation

D) Cronkhite–Canada Syndrome

• Non-hereditary
• Occurs in older adults
• Associated with alopecia, nail changes, and diarrhea
questions.learning: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome Classic Triad of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome 1. Hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine (especially jejunum) 2.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented with fever, headaches, myalgia, and drowsiness. He later developed dizziness and altered consciousness. His mother reports that he had consumed palm fruit on their recent trip to Kerala and has not been feeling well since then. Keeping the patient's history in mind, which of the following viruses should be considered in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nipah virus

This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus.

Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus, which is transmitted by animals to humans.

It is an emerging paramyxovirus that belongs to the genus Henipavirus. It has caused disease in humans who have had contact with infected animals.

It has a wide range of hosts and is associated with high mortality rates. Its natural host is a certain species of fruit bat while pigs may be an intermediate host for transmission to humans.
Its transmission can occur by the following methods:

* Unprotected exposure to the secretions from the pigs, or unprotected contact with the tissue of a sick animal.

* Consumption of fruits or fruit products (such as raw date palm juice) contaminated with urine or saliva from infected fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae.

* Human-to-human transmission through close contact with people's secretions and excretions.

* The incubation period ranges from 4 to 14 days.

Patients present with symptoms of headaches, myalgia, vomiting, and sore throat. This is followed by the onset of encephalitis, which manifests as dizziness, drowsiness, and altered consciousness. Patients may also present with acute respiratory distress. Encephalitis and seizures occur in severe cases, progressing to coma within 24 to 48 hours.

Diagnosis is by means of real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from bodily fluids and antibody detection via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods. The virus can be isolated by cell culture.

There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care.
questions.learning: Nipah virus — This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evolocumab

Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor.

PCSK9 refers to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9. They are mainly involved in the downregulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors in the liver.

Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK-9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin). Inhibition of PCSK-9 prevents the degradation of LDL receptors and thus increases LDL-cholesterol clearance by the liver. They are used in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) to decrease LDL levels.

Side effects of PCSK9 inhibitors are injection-site reactions, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, and upper respiratory tract infection and it does not increase the risk of myopathy.

Other options:

Option B: Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption by enterocytes in the small intestine. It lowers the total and LDL-C levels.

Option C: Bempedoic acid inhibits adenosine triphosphate-citrate lyase (ACL) and results in decreased LDL in patients not responding to statin therapy.

Option D: Clofibrate binds to PPAR-alpha and causes stimulation of fatty acid oxidation and increased LPL synthesis. This results in reduced triglycerides, LDL and increased high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels. It causes myopathy when combined with statins and is associated with an increased risk of gallstone formation.
questions.learning: Evolocumab Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor. PCSK9 refers to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A male patient presents with nasal obstruction, foul-smelling nasal discharge, and loss of smell. Endoscopic findings are shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrophic rhinitis

The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and the endoscopic findings points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known. It is more common in females and starts around puberty.

Clinically patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, and merciful anosmia. Merciful anosmia is when the patient has marked anosmia and is unable to smell the foul odor coming from their nose.

On examination of the nose, greenish or greyish crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. The roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment:

* Nasal irrigation - using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate 1 part, sodium biborate 1 part, sodium chloride 2 parts in 280 mL of water.

* Local antibiotics - Kemicetine antiozena solution containing chloromycetin, estradiol, and vitamin D2.

* 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, systemic use of streptomycin, potassium iodide, placental extract.

* Surgical management:

* Young's operation: In this procedure, flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both the nostrils are completely closed and are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa may revert to normal and the crusting is reduced.

* Modified Young's operation: In this procedure, the nostrils are partially closed and thereby avoiding the discomfort of complete closure of the nostrils. The results are the same compared to Young's operation.

* Narrowing of the nasal cavity can be done by submucosal injection of Teflon paste, or by insertion of fat, cartilage, or Teflon strips under the mucoperiosteum.

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps. They present with a polypoid mass in the nose.

Option C: Allergic rhinitis is associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy and can cause chronic nasal obstruction. It is characterized by watery nasal discharge, sneezing, and itching in the nose.

Option D: Foreign body nose is commonly seen in children. The child presents with unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge.
questions.learning: Atrophic rhinitis — The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and the endoscopic findings points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis. Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the given graph of effect vs dose, the orange line represents drug A which is acetylcholine. Identify drug B.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Physostigmine

The correct answer is A. Physostigmine

Interpretation of the graph:

• Orange (Drug A = Acetylcholine) → baseline dose–response
• Blue (A + B):

• ↑ Maximal effect (↑ Emax)
• Leftward/upward shift → potentiation of ACh effect

• Green (A + C):

• ↓ Emax → suggests antagonism (likely noncompetitive)

Why Physostigmine?

• Physostigmine = Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
• It prevents breakdown of acetylcholine
• Result:

• ↑ concentration of ACh at synapse
• Enhanced efficacy (↑ Emax) → matches blue curve

Why not others?

• Bethanechol → direct agonist → would produce parallel curve, not enhance ACh curve like this
• Atropine → competitive antagonist → right shift without ↓ Emax
• Adrenaline → different receptor system (adrenergic), no potentiation of ACh

Key pharmacology takeaway:

• ↑ Emax = increased efficacy → enzyme inhibition or synergistic mechanism
• Classic example:

ACh + Physostigmine → potentiation curve (blue)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding instrumental delivery, all of the following statements are correct except:
options: Vacuum is applied at the flexion point
Vacuum can be used for mentoanterior face presentation
Forceps are preferred in fetal distress
Forceps cause more maternal injury than vacuum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vacuum can be used for mentoanterior face presentation

Vacuum is contraindicated in:

• Mentoanterior face presentation
• Prematurity
• After-coming head of breech

High-yield comparison

| Vacuum | Forceps

| ------ | -------

| More fetal injury | More maternal injury

| Can rotate fetal head | Better for rapid delivery

| Can be applied at ≥6 cm dilatation | Requires full dilatation

| Contraindicated in prematurity | Preferred in preterm

Forceps preferred in:

• Fetal distress
• Maternal heart disease
• Delivery of head in breech
• Preterm baby
