questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are positive indicators for breech vaginal delivery?
options: Fetal weight less than 1.5 kg, flexed fetal head, frank breech
Frank breech, fetal weight more than 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
Frank breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
Flexed breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Frank breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks

Vaginal breech delivery may be considered when the fetus has favorable characteristics:

• Frank breech presentation → hips flexed and knees extended; generally favorable.
• Estimated fetal weight 1.5–3.5 kg → avoids the increased risks associated with very small or macrosomic fetuses.
• Gestational age >34 weeks → better developed fetus with a lower risk of complications related to prematurity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fetal weight less than 1.5 kg, flexed fetal head, frank breech → Very low birth weight/prematurity is unfavorable for planned vaginal breech delivery.
• B. Frank breech, fetal weight more than 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks → Suspected macrosomia increases the risk of difficult delivery and head entrapment.
• D. Flexed breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks → Not the classic favorable breech type; frank breech is preferred.
questions.learning: Frank breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks Vaginal breech delivery may be considered when the fetus has favorable characteristics: • Frank breech presentation → hips flexed and knees extended; generally favorable. •…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling in MCP joints and his serum uric acid levels were increased.The doctor prescribed a medicine which is considered as the first line agent in the management of this condition. What is the mechanism of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xanthine oxidase inhibitor

Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

It prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid reducing plasma uric acid levels. Allopurinol is also a substrate for xanthine oxidase. The metabolite of allopurinol called oxypurinol is a non-competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

Febuxostat is a uric acid synthesis inhibitor that acts by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase and it is indicated in gout management.

Both Febuxostat and Allopurinol are Xanthine Oxidase inhibitors, of which Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog.
questions.learning: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of the Bishop score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type of maternal pelvis

The type of maternal pelvis is not a component of the Bishop score.

The Bishop score is a scoring system used to assess labor induction outcomes. It is based on the station of the head, dilation, effacement (or length), position, and consistency of the cervix noted by doing a vaginal examination.

Note: In the modified Bishop score (1991), the effacement is replaced by the cervical length in cm.
questions.learning: Type of maternal pelvis — The type of maternal pelvis is not a component of the Bishop score. The Bishop score is a scoring system used to assess labor induction outcomes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a one-month history of lethargy, headache, fever, and vomiting. Shortly after being admitted to the hospital, the patient tragically passes away. Radiological imaging reveals multiple cystic lesions in the cerebrum with invasion into the ventricles and subarachnoid space. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neurocysticercosis

The given clinical scenario along with CT showing cystic lesions in the brain, particularly within the cerebrum, ventricles, and subarachnoid space is clearly suggestive of neurocysticercosis.

Neurocysticercosis is a form of cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium.

It usually presents with seizures and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, including headache, nausea, vomiting, vision changes, dizziness, ataxia, or confusion. Papilledema may develop secondary to hydrocephalus.

Diagnosis is done by demonstrating eggs of Taenia in faecal examination.

A biopsy of the brain or spinal cord lesion or fundoscopic visualization of subretinal cysticercus can also be done.

Imaging shows a scolex within a cystic lesion, cystic lesions with or without enhancement (e.g., ring enhancement), nodular calcifications, focal enhancing lesions, or multilobulated cystic lesions in the subarachnoid space.

Treatment of intestinal T. solium infection is by a single dose of praziquantel. Neurocysticercosis is treated with anti-epileptic drugs, anticysticidal drugs like albendazole or praziquantel, and steroids given before anticysticidal therapy.

Other options:

Option B: Astrocytoma is a type of glial cell tumour in the brain, ranging from low to high grade. They do not typically present as multiple cystic lesions and are more likely to appear as a single mass with variable enhancement on imaging.

Option C: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a congenital vascular anomaly characterized by a tangle of abnormal blood vessels connecting arteries and veins. AVMs are more likely to cause hemorrhage or seizures and typically appear as highly vascular lesions on imaging, not as cystic lesions.

Option D: While metastases can present as multiple lesions on imaging, they usually appear solid rather than cystic masses and often enhance with contrast.
questions.learning: Neurocysticercosis — The given clinical scenario along with CT showing cystic lesions in the brain, particularly within the cerebrum, ventricles, and subarachnoid space is clearly suggestive of neurocysticercosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to OPD with a history of URTI. He also has features of mouth breathing, sleep apnoea and nasal obstruction. The mother has noticed that the child increases the volume while watching TV. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, sleep apnoea, nasal obstruction, and decreased hearing points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion would be the most appropriate management.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterized by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably, rhinolalia clausa (hypo-nasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections). Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Grommet insertion alone will help resolve otitis media but the primary pathology of adenoid hypertrophy will not be addressed.

Option C: Myringotomy with grommet insertion- Myringotomy will relieve the glue ear but will not address adenoids and lead to the recurrence of symptoms.

Option D: Myringotomy involves creating a small incision in the eardrum that will relieve the otitis media but symptoms will recur due to persistent adenoid hypertrophy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, sleep apnoea, nasal obstruction, and decreased hearing points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: At what age do frontal sinuses typically become visible on an X-ray?
questions.explanation: The frontal sinuses are absent at birth and develop gradually during childhood. Although their development begins around 2 years of age, they are not radiologically visible at that stage because they are too small and poorly pneumatized. Frontal sinuses typically become visible on X-ray around 4 years of age, when sufficient pneumatization (air filling) has occurred. After this, they continue to grow and enlarge throughout childhood and adolescence, reaching full size after puberty. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 1 year: Frontal sinuses are not developed at all (B) 2 years: Development begins, but not visible on X-ray (C) 3 years: May start forming but still usually not clearly visible radiologically
questions.learning: The frontal sinuses are absent at birth and develop gradually during childhood. Although their development begins around 2 years of age, they are not radiologically visible at that stage because they are too small and poorly pneumatized.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A ten-year-old boy was brought to the OPD with fever and swelling of hands after playing football. He gives a history of previous episodes of swelling of hands. On imaging, his spleen was found to be shrunken. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sickle cell anaemia

The findings of episodes of swelling of hands (dactylitis) along with the shrunken spleen (auto splenectomy or splenic infarction) are suggestive of sickle cell disease. Moreover, the symptoms were seen after playing football, which acts as a predisposing factor to sickling to which dehydration, infection and acidosis are the triggers.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

The cardinal clinical feature of sickle cell anemia is acute vaso-occlusive pain, due to ischemia of the tissues. Vaso-occlusive crisis can cause dactylitis, splenic infarction (shrunken spleen over time) and avascular necrosis (AVN).

Most commonly, the femoral head is affected in AVN. Other sites affected include the humeral head and mandible.

Dactylitis, referred to as a hand-foot syndrome, is often the first manifestation of pain in infants and young children with sickle cell anemia. Dactylitis often manifests with symmetric or unilateral swelling of the hands and/or feet.

Other manifestations include:

• Acute splenic sequestration due to venous obstruction, needing emergency transfusion/splenectomy
• Painful ischemic crises due to vaso-occlusion in connective and musculoskeletal tissue
• Renal papillary necrosis leading to isosthenuria
• Cerebrovascular strokes
• Chronic lower leg ulcers
• Priapism in males
questions.learning: Sickle cell anaemia — The findings of episodes of swelling of hands (dactylitis) along with the shrunken spleen (auto splenectomy or splenic infarction) are suggestive of sickle cell disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with diabetes and COPD developed post-operative urinary retention. Which of the following drugs can be used for short-term treatment of the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tamsulosin

Tamsulosin is the drug used to relieve the symptoms in cases of postoperative urinary retention in a patient with COPD.

It is also efficacious in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with little effect on blood pressure.

Option B: Bethanechol is the drug of choice to relieve the symptoms in cases of postoperative urinary retention. However, it can cause bronchoconstriction in patients with COPD. Hence tamsulosin is the best answer here.

Option C: Terazosin is an α1 receptor antagonist, used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

Option D: Methacholine is a muscarinic agonist but acts specifically on bronchial smooth muscle causing its contraction. It is available as an inhalational agent and is used for the diagnosis of bronchial hyper-reactivity in patients who do not have clinically apparent asthma.
questions.learning: Tamsulosin Tamsulosin is the drug used to relieve the symptoms in cases of postoperative urinary retention in a patient with COPD. It is also efficacious in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with little effect on blood pressure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents with a palpable, firm, movable lump in her left breast, confirmed as benign on mammography. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The presentation of a palpable, firm, and highly movable breast mass (colloquially known as a "breast mouse") in a 23-year-old woman is characteristic of a fibroadenoma . Once the benign nature of the lesion has been established through clinical exam and imaging (mammogram or ultrasound), the most appropriate management for a small, asymptomatic fibroadenoma is reassurance and regular follow-up (Option B). Immediate surgical excision (Option C) is generally only indicated if the mass is rapidly growing, painful, or large ( cm), or if the patient requests it for cosmetic reasons. A biopsy (Option A) might be considered for definitive confirmation, but in a low-risk 23-year-old with classic benign features on imaging, it is not the mandatory "next" step. Tamoxifen (Option D) is used for breast cancer treatment, not benign lesions. Therefore, conservative observation is the definitive standard of care for simple fibroadenomas
questions.learning: The presentation of a palpable, firm, and highly movable breast mass (colloquially known as a "breast mouse") in a 23-year-old woman is characteristic of a fibroadenoma .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the following LV pressure-volume loop diagram, point C denotes ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic valve opens

The aortic valve will open at point C.

The volume-pressure curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle. The relationship between ventricular pressure (Y-axis) and volume (X-axis) throughout the cardiac cycle is represented by this loop.

* A - Mitral valve opens

* B - Mitral valve closes

* C - Aortic valve opens

* D - Aortic valve closes

Phase I: Period of filling

It begins at a ventricular volume of about 50 ml (end-systolic volume) and a diastolic pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg. As venous blood flows into the ventricle from the left atrium, the ventricular volume normally increases to about 120 ml, called the end-diastolic volume and the diastolic pressure rising to about 5 to 7 mm Hg.

Phase II: Period of isovolumic contraction

During isovolumic contraction, the volume of the ventricle does not change because all valves are closed. However, the pressure inside the ventricle increases to equal the pressure in the aorta (80 mm Hg) as depicted by point C.

Phase III: Period of ejection

During ejection, the systolic pressure rises even higher because of still more contraction of the ventricle. At the same time, the volume of the ventricle decreases because the aortic valve has now opened and blood flows out of the ventricle into the aorta.

Phase IV: Period of isovolumic relaxation

At the end of the period of ejection (point D), the aortic valve closes and the ventricular pressure falls back to the diastolic pressure level. The line labeled “IV” traces this decrease in intraventricular pressure without any change in volume. Thus, the ventricle returns to its starting point, with about 50 ml of blood left in the ventricle and at an atrial pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg.

The area subtended by this functional volume-pressure diagram (the shaded area, labeled “EW”) represents the net external work output of the ventricle during its contraction cycle.
questions.learning: Aortic valve opens — The aortic valve will open at point C. The volume-pressure curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Following a fall in the bathroom, an elderly lady is diagnosed with a fractured neck of the femur. Which of the following coexisting conditions is most likely to have predisposed to this injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoporosis

Given the clinical history of an elderly woman experiencing a fracture following a trivial fall, which indicates a pathological fracture, the most probable predisposing condition would be osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disorder characterized by abnormally low bone mass, which makes the bone unusually fragile and increases the risk of fractures.

A DEXA scan is performed in the following patients to assess bone mineral density and screen for osteoporosis, and the results are reported in terms of T-score or Z-score:

• Females aged 65 years or more
• Males aged 70 years or more
• Post-menopausal females under the age of 65 years with risk factors
• Fracture after the age of 50 years
• Males aged 50-69 with risk factors
questions.learning: Osteoporosis Given the clinical history of an elderly woman experiencing a fracture following a trivial fall, which indicates a pathological fracture, the most probable predisposing condition would be osteoporosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Which of the following drugs used in this condition act as prostacyclin receptor agonists? 1. Epoprostenol 2. Iloprost 3. Ambrisentan 4. Selexipag
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 4

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a story of:

• Vasoconstriction
• Endothelial dysfunction
• Vascular remodeling

The imbalance:

| Vasodilators ↓ | Vasoconstrictors ↑

| -------------- | ------------------

| Prostacyclin (PGI₂) ↓ | Endothelin-1 ↑

| Nitric oxide ↓ | Thromboxane ↑

Treatment targets these pathways like a three-pronged attack.

| Class | Drugs | Mechanism

| ----- | ----- | ---------

| Prostacyclin analogs / agonists | Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag | Vasodilation, ↓ proliferation

| Endothelin receptor antagonists | Ambrisentan, Bosentan | Block vasoconstriction

| PDE-5 inhibitors | Sildenafil, Tadalafil | ↑ NO → vasodilation

| Pathway | Drug Example | Mnemonic

| Prostacyclin | Epoprostenol | “PROS-tacyclin = PROS vasodilation”

| Endothelin | Ambrisentan | “Endothelin = enemy constrictor”

| NO pathway | Sildenafil | “Sildenafil = smooth flow”

• Prostacyclin drugs = Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag
• Ambrisentan = NOT prostacyclin (endothelin blocker)
• PAH = 3 major pathways targeted
• Severe PAH → IV prostacyclin (life-saving)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are included under diagnostic criteria of severe acute malnutrition except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Height for age

Height for age is not a diagnostic criterion of severe acute malnutrition.

Criteria for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in a 6-month-old child are mid-upper arm circumference, symmetrical pedal edema , and weight for height. Height for age is not the criteria for the diagnosis of severe acute malnutrition.

The presence of any of the following confers severe acute malnutrition in children 6 to 59 months of age:

1. Weight-for-height below -3 standard deviation (<-3SD) on the WHO Growth Standard (Option B)
2. Presence of bipedal edema  (Option C)
3. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 11.5 cm (Option D)

Once the child is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition, the doctor must assess for the following complications:

1. Severe edema (+++)
2. Low appetite (failed appetite test)
3. Medical complications (severe anemia, pneumonia, diarrhea, dehydration, cerebral palsy, tuberculosis, HIV, heart disease, etc.)
One or more danger signs as per IMNCI

If any of the complications are present, the child is diagnosed with complicated SAM and is managed inpatient in the facility.

If the above-mentioned signs are absent, the child is diagnosed with uncomplicated SAM and supervised management at home is given.
questions.learning: Height for age Height for age is not a diagnostic criterion of severe acute malnutrition. Criteria for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in a 6-month-old child are mid-upper arm circumference, symmetrical pedal edema , and weight for height.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents to the outpatient department with right testicular pain following a blow from a cricket ball two hours earlier. Examination reveals severe testicular tenderness and absence of the cremasteric reflex. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of sudden, severe testicular pain following trauma, combined with an absent cremasteric reflex, are highly suggestive of testicular torsion. While trauma is the inciting event, the clinical signs point toward vascular compromise of the spermatic cord. Current guidelines recommend an urgent USG Arterial Doppler as the first diagnostic step to assess blood flow. An absence of arterial flow confirms torsion and necessitates immediate surgery. NSAIDs (Option B) only provide symptomatic relief and would dangerously delay the diagnosis of a surgical emergency. Venous Doppler (Option C) is less reliable for confirming the arterial ischemia that defines torsion. Although surgical exploration (Option D) is the definitive treatment, the trauma history lowers the pre-test probability slightly, making Doppler the preferred initial confirmatory investigation. Timely detorsion within the 6-hour "golden period" is essential to ensure testicular salvage
questions.learning: The clinical findings of sudden, severe testicular pain following trauma, combined with an absent cremasteric reflex, are highly suggestive of testicular torsion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with complaints of ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. A diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. III, IV, V(1), VI

In Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome, Cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (Trochlear nerve), VI (Abducens nerve), and V1 (Ophthalmic division of the Trigeminal nerve) get compressed causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and sensory loss in the V1 area.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face. The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the following:

* Pain, typically labeled as retro–orbital ache

* Sensory loss/disturbances in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the 5th cranial nerve

* Ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia due to the involvement of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerves involvement

* Ptosis, due to 3rd nerve paralysis

Trauma affecting the orbital region is the most common cause of superior orbital fissure syndrome. Other causes include infections such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, inflammatory disorders, and tumors. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by imaging modalities like CT or MRI to identify the underlying pathology. Management depends on the cause and may involve surgical decompression, corticosteroid therapy, or antiviral treatment.

Pearl PF0436: Superior orbital fissure

Structures passing through the Superior orbital fissure

Above the common tendinous ring: LFT (Superolateral compartment)

* Lacrimal nerve

* Frontal nerve

* Trochlear nerve

* Superior opthalmic vein

Within the common tendinous ring: BAN (Intermediate compartment)

* Both divisions of oculomotor nerve

* Abducens nerve

* Nasociliary nerve

Below the common tendinous ring (Inferomedial compartment)

* Inferior ophthalmic vein

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year-old female patient presented with malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and multiple joint pain. She has no relevant past history and does not take any medication. On further investigations, thrombocytopenia was seen and the Anti-Sm antibody was positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Systemic Lupus Erythematous

The clinical scenario along with Anti-Sm antibody positivity is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

SLE is an autoimmune disease that mostly affects women of reproductive age. It is characterized by the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes that cause widespread systemic damage.

Diagnosis of SLE requires at least four of the following categories:

Clinical features:

* Skin:

* acute, subacute cutaneous manifestations (photosensitivity, malar or maculopapular rash)

* chronic cutaneous manifestations (discoid lupus, panniculitis, lichen planus like)

* Oral or nasal ulcers

* Nonscarring alopecia

* Synovitis involving 2 or more joints

* Serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis)

* Renal:

* Protein/Creatinine ratio of more than 0.5

* RBC casts

* Biopsy

* Neurologic: seizures, psychosis, myelitis, neuropathy, confusional state

* Hemolytic anemia

* Leukopenia/lymphopenia

* Thrombocytopenia

Immunological manifestations:

* Antinuclear antibodies > reference value

* Anti-dsDNA > reference value

* Anti Smith antibody

* Antiphospholipid antibody (lupus anticoagulant, false-positive rapid plasma reagin)

* Low serum complement

* Positive direct Coombs' test in absence of hemolytic anemia.

Four criteria with one in each category must be positive for it to qualify as a diagnosis of SLE. However, if a renal biopsy is suggestive of lupus nephritis and lupus autoantibodies are positive then four criteria are not required.

questions.learning: Systemic Lupus Erythematous — The clinical scenario along with Anti-Sm antibody positivity is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLE is an autoimmune disease that mostly affects women of reproductive age.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old infant is rushed to the emergency room with lethargy, vomiting, convulsions, and poor feeding following a period of prolonged fasting. Laboratory results revealed hypoglycemia, low ketone bodies, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following metabolic defects is most likely in this infant?
options: Medium chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medium chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a 3-year-old child with non-ketotic hypoglycaemia and mild hepatosplenomegaly suggests medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCAD), in which there is impaired beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids (in the mitochondria), which leads to the accumulation of dicarboxylic acids due to increased microsomal omega oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids.

In MCAD deficiency, there is impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids. This results in decreased ATP and acetyl CoA levels. The low acetyl CoA levels reduce pyruvate carboxylase activity (as acetyl CoA is its allosteric activator), causing decreased gluconeogenesis and fasting hypoglycemia. Additionally, low acetyl CoA levels impair ketone body synthesis, leading to non-ketotic hypoglycemia.
Due to the impaired beta-oxidation, medium-chain fatty acids undergo increased omega-oxidation in the microsomes, leading to the accumulation and subsequent urinary excretion of medium-chain C6-C10 ω-dicarboxylic acids.

Clinical features:

* Non-ketotic hypoglycemia, particularly during fasting or metabolic stress.

* Potential for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) due to severe metabolic derangements.

* Symptoms of lethargy, vomiting, and seizures during periods of fasting or illness.

Laboratory findings:

* Hypoglycaemia with low or absent ketone bodies.

* Elevated levels of dicarboxylic acids (C6-C10) in urine due to omega oxidation.

* Abnormal acylcarnitine profile: Due to defective medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, medium-chain fatty acids (C6-C12) cannot undergo beta-oxidation. These fatty acids accumulate and are converted to acylcarnitines, leading to an abnormal acylcarnitine profile characterised by elevated levels of medium-chain acylcarnitines (e.g., C6, C8, C10).

Management:

* Prevent fasting: Ensure frequent carbohydrate-rich meals to avoid hypoglycaemia.

* Emergency glucose supplementation: During illness or fasting to prevent metabolic crises.

* Dietary modification: Avoid medium-chain triglycerides and focus on long-chain fatty acids.

Other options:

Option A:  Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (HFI):

* Genetics: Autosomal recessive disorder. Mutations in the ALDOB gene leading to aldolase B deficiency.

* Onset: Patients remain asymptomatic until fructose or sucrose is ingested. Eg: fruits, fruit juice, sweetened cereals, table sugar.

* Clinical features:

* Jaundice

* Hepatomegaly

* Vomiting

* Lethargy and irritability

* Convulsions

Option C: Hers disease (type VI glycogen storage disorder) – It is caused by the deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase. Patients with Hers disease exhibit growth retardation, hepatomegaly, and mild hypoglycaemia.

Option D: von Gierke disease is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, and patients with this condition have hypoglycaemia, lactic acidaemia, ketosis, hyperlipidaemia and liver and renal tubule cells having glycogen deposits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old male child presented with fever, fatigue and left ventricular dysfunction. He underwent a cardiac biopsy (image shown). Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lymphocytic myocarditis

The biopsy shows interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates with myocyte injury, characteristic of lymphocytic myocarditis.

It commonly follows a viral infection and presents with fever, fatigue, and acute LV dysfunction in children.

Acute rheumatic fever shows Aschoff bodies, Chagas has amastigotes, and pyogenic myocarditis shows neutrophilic infiltration.

A) Acute rheumatic fever

Histology would show: Aschoff bodies

Not lymphocytic myocarditis.

C) Chagas disease

Caused by: Trypanosoma cruzi

Histology shows parasites inside myocytes.

D) Pyogenic myocarditis

Would show neutrophilic infiltration and abscess formation.
questions.learning: Lymphocytic myocarditis — The biopsy shows interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates with myocyte injury, characteristic of lymphocytic myocarditis. It commonly follows a viral infection and presents with fever, fatigue, and acute LV dysfunction in children.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with chronic diarrhea shows the following CT appearance. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulcerative colitis

Why is this CT suggestive of Ulcerative Colitis?

The key imaging feature is a featureless, shortened colon with loss of haustrations, producing the classic:

"Lead-pipe colon" appearance

• Normal colon has sacculations called haustra.
• Chronic inflammation in UC causes:

• Mucosal ulceration
• Muscular hypertrophy
• Fibrosis
• Loss of haustra

• The colon becomes smooth, rigid, and tubular → Lead-pipe appearance.

This is a classic radiological sign of chronic ulcerative colitis.

Why not the other options?

B. Tubercular Colitis

CT usually shows:

• Ileocecal involvement (most common)
• Asymmetric wall thickening
• Necrotic mesenteric lymph nodes
• Pulled-up contracted cecum

Loss of haustra involving long segments of colon is not typical.

C. Crohn's Disease

CT findings:

• Skip lesions
• Terminal ileal involvement
• Cobblestone appearance
• Fistulas and sinus tracts
• Creeping fat
• String sign

Crohn's causes segmental disease, whereas UC causes continuous colonic involvement.

D. Pseudomembranous Colitis

CT shows:

• Marked colonic wall thickening
• Accordion sign
• Thumbprinting
• Toxic megacolon in severe cases
•

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true with respect to the Little's area?
options: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum.
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

The correct statement among the following is Option A, Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

Little's area:

Little’s area, situated at the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum is the most common site of epistaxis in children and young adults. 90% of bleeds arise from Little's area, where the Kiesselbach plexus is situated on the nasal septum.

Factors that increase the risk of epistaxis in children when compared to adults, include the habit of nose picking and increased friability of mucosa due to frequent upper respiratory tract infections.

Kiesselbach’s plexus:

Four arteries anastomose at the anterior inferior part of the nasal septum (Little's area) to form a vascular plexus called Kiesselbach’s plexus.

* Anterior ethmoidal

* Septal branch of the superior labial

* Septal branch of sphenopalatine

* Septal branch of the greater palatine
questions.learning: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area. The correct statement among the following is Option A, Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which muscle pairs are responsible for levo depression?
questions.explanation: Levo depression means depression of both eyes when looking to the left (levoversion). In left gaze, the left eye is abducted and the right eye is adducted. 1. The left eye (abducted) is depressed mainly by the Left Inferior Rectus (LIR). 2. The right eye (adducted) is depressed mainly by the Right Superior Oblique (RSO). Thus, the correct muscle pair is RSO (right superior oblique) and LIR (left inferior rectus). Why other options are wrong: (A) LSO and RIR: These muscles produce depression in the opposite gaze combination (not levo depression). (C) RIO and LIR: Inferior oblique elevates the eye, not depresses it. (D) LIO and RIR: Inferior oblique again causes elevation, and the pairing does not match left gaze depression
questions.learning: Levo depression means depression of both eyes when looking to the left (levoversion). In left gaze, the left eye is abducted and the right eye is adducted.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding pelvic cellular tissue? 1. It supports the pelvic organs. 2. It forms protective sheath for blood vessels and terminal part of ureter. 3. It prevents infection to be spread out of pelvis. 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Pelvic cellular tissue (endopelvic connective tissue) is a loose fibro-fatty connective tissue located between the pelvic fascia.

• 1. It supports the pelvic organs. ✓

• Pelvic cellular tissue helps support the uterus, cervix, vagina, bladder, and rectum, maintaining normal pelvic anatomy.

• 2. It forms a protective sheath for blood vessels and the terminal part of the ureter. ✓

• It encloses the uterine vessels, pelvic vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and terminal ureter, providing support and protection.

• 3. It prevents infection from spreading out of the pelvis. ✗

• Incorrect. Pelvic cellular tissue actually contains potential spaces through which infection (pelvic cellulitis/parametritis), hemorrhage, and malignant cells can spread.

• 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. ✓

• Under the influence of estrogen and progesterone, pelvic connective tissue becomes hypertrophied, edematous, and more vascular, facilitating uterine enlargement and childbirth.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Researchers are studying the prevalence of intravenous drug use in a large metropolitan area. Because this is a stigmatized and hard-to-reach population, investigators initially identify a small group of participants through community outreach programs. Each participant is then asked to refer friends or acquaintances who also use intravenous drugs, and those referrals are further asked to recruit others. The sample gradually expands until the desired sample size is reached. Which of the following best describes the sampling strategy used in this study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Snowball sampling

Snowball sampling is a non-probability sampling method used to recruit participants from hidden, stigmatized, or hard-to-reach populations such as intravenous drug users, sex workers, or undocumented immigrants. Initial participants recruit additional subjects from their personal networks, causing the sample to expand progressively.

Key features:

• Useful when a formal sampling frame is unavailable
• Cost-effective for rare populations
• Recruitment depends on participant referrals

Major limitation: High risk of selection bias and limited generalizability because participants are not selected randomly.

Comparison with other methods:

• Simple random sampling → every individual has equal chance of selection
• Stratified sampling → population divided into subgroups before random sampling
• Cluster sampling → random selection of naturally occurring groups/clusters.
questions.learning: Snowball sampling Snowball sampling is a non-probability sampling method used to recruit participants from hidden, stigmatized, or hard-to-reach populations such as intravenous drug users, sex workers, or undocumented immigrants.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the underlying cause of hypoxia in a newly arrived resident in a high-altitude region?
questions.explanation: At high altitudes, the total barometric pressure decreases, which results in a corresponding decrease in the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2). This lower PO2 in the atmosphere leads to a lower PO2 in the alveoli and consequently in the arterial blood, causing hypoxia. This is the primary physiological challenge for anyone ascending to high altitudes. Low hemoglobin levels (Option A, anemia) can cause hypoxia, but it is not the cause of altitude-related distress; in fact, the body eventually increases hemoglobin as an adaptation. Low blood lactate (Option C) is not a cause of hypoxia. High partial pressure of CO2 (Option D) would indicate hypoventilation, but at high altitudes, residents typically hyperventilate to compensate for the low oxygen, leading to low CO2 levels. Understanding this fundamental relationship between atmospheric pressure and PO2 is essential for grasping the pathophysiology of acute mountain sickness and the subsequent process of acclimatization
questions.learning: At high altitudes, the total barometric pressure decreases, which results in a corresponding decrease in the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of recurrent, large-volume, watery diarrhea. She reports experiencing multiple episodes per day, often waking her at night. She has also noted significant weight loss and episodes of muscle weakness. Laboratory findings reveal hypokalemia. Imaging studies of the abdomen show a mass in the tail of the pancreas. Which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIPoma

This patient with recurrent, large-volume, watery diarrhea with laboratory evidence of hypokalemia and a mass in the pancreatic tail is most likely afflicted by a VIPoma.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumours (VIPomas) are  pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptides (VIP) which are responsible for the secretory watery diarrhoea and other symptoms. The patient commonly presents with severe intermittent watery diarrhoea leading to dehydration, and weakness from fluid and electrolyte losses.

Electrolyte abnormalities in VIPoma include:

* Metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia- due to a large amount of GI loss and bicarbonate wasting

* Hypochlorhydria- due to the direct gastric acid inhibitory effect of VIP

* Hypomagnesemia- due to severe diarrhoea

* Hyperglycemia- due to the increased glycogenolytic activity of VIP

* Hypercalcemia- due to dehydration, coincidental MEN1 syndrome, or secretion by the tumor of a calcitrophic peptide

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumor (VIPoma) is also referred to as Verner–Morrison syndrome/ WDHA syndrome:

WDHA stands for:

* WD - Watery Diarrhea

* H – Hypokalemia

* A – Achlorhydria

Metastases commonly occurs in the liver, lymph nodes, bones, and kidney.

Diagnosis can be made by the demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level (upto 250 to 500 pg/ml) and a history of large-volume diarrhea (> 5L/day). A CT scan localizes most VIPomas. EUS is the most sensitive imaging method.

While suspecting a case of VIPoma it is essential to conduct a VIP assay so as to confirm the presence of other tumors of neural crest origin such as neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma.

The medical management of VIPoma:

*

Initial medical management is symptomatic with correction of fluids and electrolyte imbalance.

*

Somatostatin analogs like octreotide and lanreotide inhibit secretion of VIP and are used for symptomatic control.

*

Glucocorticoids are used in patients refractory to somatostatin analogs.

*

Interferon-alpha has also been used in patients in patients not responding to the above medications.

The surgical management of VIPoma:

* Complete resection is the treatment of choice for primary tumors and is usually a distal pancreatectomy. If the tumor cannot be excised completely, surgical debulkingmay be done

* Radiofrequency ablation and cryoablation

* Hepatic artery embolization is a palliative treatment measure in patients with unresectable hepatic metastases.

* Islet hyperplasia (previously known as nesidioblastosis) is seen in maternal diabetes, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome , and rare mutations in the β-cell K+-channel protein or sulfonylurea receptor.

* In maternal diabetes, the fetal islets respond to hyperglycemia by increasing their size and number. In the postnatal period, these hyperactive islets may be responsible for serious episodes of hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents during a routine antenatal visit with sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and reduced fetal movements. She also has a history of hypertension during the current pregnancy. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of sudden onset "severe abdominal pain," "vaginal bleeding," and a "history of hypertension" in the third trimester is highly characteristic of abruptio placenta. Placental abruption involves the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall. The pain results from the accumulation of blood behind the placenta (retroplacental hematoma) and uterine contractions. Placenta previa (Option B) classically presents with "painless" bright red vaginal bleeding. Hydramnios (Option C) refers to excessive amniotic fluid and causes generalized discomfort but not acute bleeding or severe pain. Preterm labor (Option D) typically presents with regular, rhythmic contractions rather than constant severe pain and significant hemorrhage. The decrease in fetal movements is a concerning sign of fetal distress or hypoxia due to compromised placental circulation. Abruptio placenta is an obstetric emergency that requires urgent assessment of maternal hemodynamic stability and fetal well-being, often necessitating emergency delivery
questions.learning: The clinical triad of sudden onset "severe abdominal pain," "vaginal bleeding," and a "history of hypertension" in the third trimester is highly characteristic of abruptio placenta.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense itching, photophobia, and ropy discharge from his eyes. Moreover, on examination the following finding is present. What is the most probable diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

The above image depicts a cobblestone appearance, and also the presence of ropy discharge points towards the diagnosis of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) or spring catarrh.

VKC is bilateral allergic conjunctivitis that is common in children above the age of 5 years and in warm dry climates such as the Mediterranean, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Middle East.

It is IgE and cell-mediated inflammation of the conjunctiva. It results in the following findings:

Palpebral disease

* Cobblestone papillae: Macropapillae (<1 mm) have a flat-topped polygonal appearance reminiscent of cobblestones

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

Limbal disease

* Horner-Trantas dots which are limbal conjunctival papillae

Keratopathy

* Superior punctate epithelial erosions

* Shield ulcers, which may develop when the exposed Bowman membrane becomes coated with mucus and calcium phosphate, leading to inadequate wetting and delayed re-epithelialization.

* Pseudogerentexon resembling arcus senilus. It has a cupid's bow outline

Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease.

Other options:

* Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms).

* Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction due to endogenous allergens like Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

* Xerophthalmia is a term used to cover all ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

Image: Horner Trantas spots

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with altered sensorium and his BP was 220/110 mmHg. He also had one episode of vomiting and on examination has weakness in the left upper and lower limbs. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: BP should be checked multiple times before administering anti-hypertensives

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with progressively worsening blurry vision, eye pain, and redness in the right eye. Examination reveals restricted eye movement, and fundoscopic evaluation identifies a well-defined cystic lesion in the vitreous humor, accompanied by surrounding inflammation. What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ocular cysticercosis

• The presence of a well-defined cystic lesion in the vitreous with surrounding inflammation is characteristic of ocular cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium larvae.
• Symptoms include progressive blurring of vision, ocular pain, redness, and restricted eye movements due to inflammatory response.

Other options:

• A. Ocular toxoplasmosis usually presents as retinochoroiditis.
• B. Endophthalmitis is a diffuse purulent infection.
• DTubercular posterior uveitis does not produce a discrete vitreous cyst.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis without any significant impairment in his daily activities. On further workup, a diagnosis of a mild case of ITP is made. How will you manage the patient?
options: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Education, counseling and watchful expectancy

In this patients with mild ITP, the next step in management is education, counselling, and watchful expectancy.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura or idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder in which there is immune-mediated destruction of platelets. The antibodies formed in the spleen against the cell-surface antigens GpIIb/IIIa or GpIb/IX, cause increased peripheral destruction of platelets. It can be

* Asymptomatic.

* Mild symptoms- bruising and petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis which has very little interference with daily living.

* Moderate symptoms- more severe skin and mucosal lesions, more troublesome epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

* Severe symptoms- bleeding episodes - menorrhagia, epistaxis, and melena - requiring transfusions or hospitalization, symptoms interfering seriously with quality of life.

Treatment of ITP:

* Mild to moderate bleeding symptoms- watchful expectancy, education, and counselling.

* Platelet count < 30,000 + risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)- oral glucocorticoids or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or IV anti-D

* Severe bleeding symptoms- IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG or IV anti-D

* Life-threatening bleeding (eg. intracranial haemorrhage)- platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or IV anti-D

The role of splenectomy in ITP should be reserved for 2 circumstances:

* The older child (≥4 yr) with severe ITP that has lasted >1 year (chronic ITP) and whose symptoms are not easily controlled with medical therapy

* When life-threatening hemorrhage (ICH) complicates acute ITP and the platelet count cannot be corrected rapidly with transfusion of platelets and administration of IVIG and corticosteroids.

It is characterized by

* Isolated thrombocytopenia—the presence of antibody against platelet membrane glycoprotein and subsequent destruction in reticuloendothelial system

* Normal bone marrow—normal or even increased number of megakaryocytes

* Absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which class of shock is there an initial decrease in urine output?
questions.explanation: Moderate shock, often corresponding to Class III hemorrhage (1500–2000 mL blood loss), is where a noticeable and initial decrease in urine output typically occurs. In this stage, the body's compensatory mechanisms, such as intense peripheral vasoconstriction and the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, prioritize blood flow to the heart and brain at the expense of the kidneys. This leads to oliguria, with urine output falling to roughly 5–15 mL/hour. In Compensated or Mild shock (Options A and C), renal perfusion is often sufficiently maintained to keep urine output within near-normal limits (usually mL/hour). In Severe shock (Option D), urine output is typically negligible (anuria), representing a late and critical stage of circulatory failure rather than the "initial" decrease. Recognizing this drop in Moderate shock is vital for clinicians to initiate aggressive fluid resuscitation to prevent irreversible renal tubular damage or progression to multi-organ failure
questions.learning: Moderate shock, often corresponding to Class III hemorrhage (1500–2000 mL blood loss), is where a noticeable and initial decrease in urine output typically occurs.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia, who did not respond to haloperidol and thioridazine, was started on drug A. After beginning treatment with drug A, the patient's psychotic symptoms improved; however, he developed sialorrhea, dyslipidemia, weight gain, and hyperglycemia. Which drug is most likely to be 'drug A'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clozapine

This patient has schizophrenia not responding to two antipsychotics (haloperidol and thioridazine). Failure to respond to two adequate trials of antipsychotics suggests treatment-resistant schizophrenia, for which clozapine is the drug of choice.

The side effects described strongly point toward clozapine:

• Sialorrhea (excessive salivation) – very characteristic adverse effect
• Weight gain – due to metabolic effects
• Dyslipidemia
• Hyperglycemia / risk of diabetes mellitus

These are part of the metabolic syndrome commonly associated with clozapine.
questions.learning: Clozapine — This patient has schizophrenia not responding to two antipsychotics (haloperidol and thioridazine). Failure to respond to two adequate trials of antipsychotics suggests treatment-resistant schizophrenia, for which clozapine is the drug of choice.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with a congenital deformity of the external ear. What is the ideal age for performing otoplasty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-6 years

Otoplasty (pinnaplasty) is ideally performed at 5–6 years of age, when:

• The external ear has reached approximately 85–90% of its adult size, allowing durable correction.
• The auricular cartilage is still soft and pliable, making surgical reshaping easier.
•

The procedure is completed before school age, helping reduce psychological distress, teasing, and bullying related to prominent or malformed ears.

•

Common indication: Prominent ears (bat ears), congenital auricular deformities (when adequate cartilage is present).

• Goal: Improve ear shape and symmetry while minimizing psychosocial impact.

questions.text: In Barrett's esophagus, which of the following epithelial transformations occurs?

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year- old woman was diagnosed with right leg cellulitis and was admitted in hospital for 3 days. She was prescribed clindamycin. Two days after her discharge, she developed diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.8 degrees. Her blood reports revealed a Hb level of 12g/dl; WBC count of 18,000/mm3; CRP of 160mg/l. What is the most probable etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clostridium difficile

The given clinical vignette of a patient with diarrhoea following antibiotic administration is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile.

Clostridium difficile is the most common cause of infectious diarrhoea in nosocomial infections. It is the most common antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. It is commonly seen in individuals who receive a prolonged antibiotic course, which causes a change in the composition of gastrointestinal microbial flora, leading to the colonization of C. difficile.

Clinical features:

* Lower abdominal pain with loose watery diarrhea.

* Fever, leukocytosis

* In some patients, the disease may progress to life-threatening pseudomembranous colitis.

Investigations:

* Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in stool

* Stool culture in selective media

* Demonstrating toxin by Hep-2 cell cultures

* Toxin gene identification by enzyme immunoassay

* Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy reveals a characteristic appearance, with erythema, white plaques, or an adherent pseudomembrane.

Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in the stool are used as they are both rapid and sensitive while retaining high specificity.

Oral vancomycin, metronidazole, and fidaxomicin are used for the treatment of pseudomembranous colitis, depending on its severity.

First choice treatment of C. difficile colitis:

Severity
Treatment

Mild to moderate
Oral Vancomycin

Severe (WBC >15,000/cu.mm, Creatinine >1.5 times baseline)
Oral Vancomycin

Severe, Complicated (Shock, Ileus, Toxic Megacolon)
Oral Vancomycin + IV Metronidazole ± Rectal Vancomycin

Recurrent/ multiple episodes
Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT)

Fidaxomicin is an alternative in all cases. Metronidazole is now reserved for non-severe infections in settings where access to first-line drugs is limited or cost is an issue.

Recent update: Harrison's 20th edition recommends the use of vancomycin over metronidazole in the treatment of initial episodes which are mild to moderate in severity. Metronidazole is recommended only if vancomycin or fidaxomicin are not accessible. Oral metronidazole is less effective than the other options and may necessitate a longer treatment course for response.

Other options: Escherichia coli, Norovirus, Rotavirus are all causes of Traveller's diarrhea.

Other causes for Nosocomial diarrhea:

* Clostridium perfringens,

* Klebsiella oxytoca,

* Staphylococcus aureus.

Pearl PF1578: Diagnostic criteria for Clostridium difficile infection

The diagnosis of CDI is based on a combination of clinical criteria:

1.Diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools per 24 h for ≥2 days) with no other recognized cause

2.Detection of toxins A or B in the stool by PCR or culture

or

Detection of pseudomembranes in the colon

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child with mental retardation, blindness, and muscle weakness was investigated and was found to be deficient for Hexosaminidase-A enzyme. She is most likely suffering from ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tay-sachs disease

Tay-Sachs disease is due to the deficiency of the enzyme Hexosaminidase A which degrades GM2 gangliosides.

Tay-Sachs disease is a rare genetic disorder characterized by the deficiency of the enzyme Hexosaminidase-A. This enzyme is responsible for breaking down a fatty substance called GM2 ganglioside, which is found primarily in nerve cells.

Without sufficient Hexosaminidase-A activity, GM2 ganglioside accumulates in the cells, particularly in the brain and nerve tissues, leading to the characteristic symptoms of Tay-Sachs disease.

Clinical features of Tay-Sachs disease are :

* Loss of motor skills

* Seizures

* Hyperacusis

* Macrocephaly

* Macular cherry-red spots

* Neurodegeneration

* Blindness

* Muscular weakness

Other options:

A. Krabbe's disease: Krabbe's disease, also known as globoid cell leukodystrophy, is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme galactosylceramidase. It leads to the accumulation of a lipid called galactocerebroside in the nervous system. The symptoms of Krabbe's disease may include muscle weakness, developmental delay, and vision problems, but mental retardation is not typically a prominent feature.

B. Fabry's disease: Fabry's disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of a fatty substance called globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in various tissues and organs. Fabry's disease can present with a wide range of symptoms, including neurological manifestations, skin abnormalities, kidney problems, and cardiovascular complications. However, mental retardation is not a typical feature of Fabry's disease.

D. Gaucher's disease: Gaucher's disease is an inherited disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of a lipid called glucocerebroside primarily in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Gaucher's disease can present with various symptoms, including hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged liver and spleen), anemia, and skeletal abnormalities. Mental retardation and blindness are not characteristic features of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The toughness of bacterial cell walls is due to:
questions.explanation: The structural integrity and toughness of the bacterial cell wall are primarily derived from the peptidoglycan layer (murein). This mesh-like polymer provides the rigidity necessary to maintain cell shape and protect the bacterium from osmotic lysis. In Gram-positive bacteria, this layer is thick (up to 100 layers), whereas in Gram-negative bacteria, it is significantly thinner. Regarding the distractors, teichoic acid (Option A) is found only in Gram-positive cell walls and contributes to stability and ion transport but does not provide primary structural strength. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) (Option C) are components of the outer membrane (Option D) found only in Gram-negative bacteria. While the outer membrane acts as a protective barrier against toxic substances, the physical "toughness" and resistance to pressure are functions of the underlying peptidoglycan. Therefore, peptidoglycan is the essential molecule responsible for the mechanical strength of the bacterial cell wall
questions.learning: The structural integrity and toughness of the bacterial cell wall are primarily derived from the peptidoglycan layer (murein). This mesh-like polymer provides the rigidity necessary to maintain cell shape and protect the bacterium from osmotic lysis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following are true about the instrument shown in the image given below except-
options: It is used for the localization of a foreign body.
It is used for the measurement of the angle of the posterior chamber.
It is used for the demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae.
It provides a mirror image of the opposite angle.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the measurement of the angle of the posterior chamber.

The given instrument is an indirect gonioscope, which is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber, i.e., for gonioscopy, and not the angle of the posterior chamber.

Types:

* Indirect gonioprism- provides mirror image of the opposite angle.

* Direct goniolens- provides a direct view of the angle

Application:

* To view the angle of the anterior chamber

* Localization of the foreign body, abnormal blood vessels, or tumors in the angle

* Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae

* Direct goniolens can be used during goniotomy

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman was admitted for three days with left leg cellulitis and treated with clindamycin. Two days after discharge, she develops abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhea. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis with raised ESR and CRP levels. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a patient developing abdominal pain and watery diarrhea shortly after hospitalization and a course of antibiotics (Clindamycin) is the classic description of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). Clindamycin is notorious for disrupting the normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile to overgrow and produce toxins that cause pseudo-membranous colitis. The elevated white cell count (leukocytosis) and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) support a bacterial inflammatory cause. E. coli (Option A) is a common gut dweller but not specifically linked to clindamycin-associated diarrhea. Norovirus (Option B) and Rotavirus (Option D) cause acute viral gastroenteritis but typically involve vomiting and occur in community outbreaks rather than specifically following antibiotic use in the elderly. Diagnosis of CDI is confirmed by stool toxin PCR or ELISA. First-line treatment involves oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
questions.learning: The clinical picture of a patient developing abdominal pain and watery diarrhea shortly after hospitalization and a course of antibiotics (Clindamycin) is the classic description of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Pressure volume loop of the left ventricle is shown below. Which of the following changes shifts the curve from ABCD to ABC’D’?
questions.explanation:

The solid loop (ABCD) represents the normal cardiac cycle, while the dashed loop (ABC’D’) shows the altered condition. This indicates an increased afterload.

Increased Peripheral Arterial Resistance (Afterload)

Effects:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During intrauterine development, the talus, a tarsal bone of the foot, begins ossification at a specific gestational age. At what time during fetal life does ossification of the talus occur?
questions.explanation: The ossification of the tarsal bones follows a specific chronological sequence during intrauterine development. The talus typically begins to ossify at 7 months of intrauterine life. It is the second tarsal bone to ossify, following the calcaneus, which begins ossification at approximately 5 to 6 months of gestation. The cuboid bone is usually the third, ossifying shortly before birth, often at 9 months. Options A (3 months), C (9 months), and D (2 months) are incorrect for the talus. While the primary centers for long bones appear much earlier (around the 8th week or 2nd month), the tarsal bones are mostly cartilaginous at birth, except for the calcaneus, talus, and sometimes the cuboid. Identifying the presence of these ossification centers on fetal radiographs or ultrasounds can be a useful clinical indicator for assessing gestational age and skeletal maturity in a developing fetus
questions.learning: The ossification of the tarsal bones follows a specific chronological sequence during intrauterine development. The talus typically begins to ossify at 7 months of intrauterine life.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presents with early satiety, marked splenomegaly extending up to the umbilicus, and clinical features of bleeding such as petechiae. Laboratory evaluation reveals a markedly elevated white blood cell count of 85,000/cu.mm, with the peripheral blood smear showing immature B-cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of massive splenomegaly (manifesting as early satiety), thrombocytopenia (leading to petechiae and bleeding), and marked leukocytosis is highly suggestive of an acute hematological malignancy. The key diagnostic clue is the presence of immature B cells (lymphoblasts) on the peripheral blood smear, which is characteristic of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). ALL is the most common leukemia in children, but it can also occur in adolescents and young adults. The malignant lymphoblasts typically express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and B-cell markers such as CD10 (CALLA), supporting the diagnosis. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML, Option A) would show myeloblasts, often with Auer rods. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML, Option B) is characterized by a full spectrum of granulocytic precursors and is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL). Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL, Option C) usually affects elderly patients and shows mature small lymphocytes. ALL is a medical emergency requiring prompt initiation of chemotherapy. Splenomegaly occurs due to infiltration of malignant cells into the reticuloendothelial system
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of massive splenomegaly (manifesting as early satiety), thrombocytopenia (leading to petechiae and bleeding), and marked leukocytosis is highly suggestive of an acute hematological malignancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If the percentage of thymine residues in DNA is 28%. What is the percentage of cytosine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 22%

The percentage of cytosine in the DNA is 22%.

As per the Chargaff's rule, in the DNA molecules, the concentration of deoxyadenosine (A) equals that of thymidine (T), and the concentration of deoxyguanosine (G) equals that of deoxycytidine (C). Therefore, A=T and G=C.

In the question, the concentration of thymine is given as 28%, therefore the concentration of adenine is also 28%, both of which add up to 56%. The remaining 44% (100-56) of the DNA consists of G-C base pairs. Of which the guanine constitutes 22% and the cytosine constitutes another 22%.
questions.learning: 22% The percentage of cytosine in the DNA is 22%. As per the Chargaff's rule, in the DNA molecules, the concentration of deoxyadenosine (A) equals that of thymidine (T), and the concentration of deoxyguanosine (G) equals that of deoxycytidine (C).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: How is a 'Case' of tuberculosis defined according to standard medical guidelines?
questions.explanation: This question is a duplicate from the source, re-emphasizing the definition of a TB case. A definitive diagnosis of tuberculosis requires the detection of the pathogen. Sputum positive status (Option B) (either by smear, culture, or molecular test) is the gold standard for defining a "microbiologically confirmed case." This is the highest priority for public health because these patients are actively shedding the bacteria. X-ray (Option A) is a screening tool used to identify lung damage. Mantoux (Option C) is an immunological test for exposure. A history of cough (Option D) for more than two weeks is the primary trigger for investigation but does not constitute a diagnosis . Modern guidelines have shifted to include "clinically diagnosed cases" where microbiology is negative but symptoms and imaging are highly suggestive, but the classic epidemiological definition for reporting still prioritizes the sputum-positive status to ensure accurate disease tracking and transmission control
questions.learning: This question is a duplicate from the source, re-emphasizing the definition of a TB case. A definitive diagnosis of tuberculosis requires the detection of the pathogen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following veins are involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to liver cirrhosis. When portal blood flow is obstructed, portosystemic anastomoses form at specific sites. At the lower end of the esophagus, the portal circulation (represented by the left gastric vein) meets the systemic circulation (represented by the esophageal veins draining into the azygos system). Increased pressure in the left gastric vein causes the submucosal esophageal veins to become dilated and tortuous, forming varices. The right gastric vein (Option B) drains the lesser curvature but is not the primary contributor to lower esophageal varices. The left gastroepiploic vein (Option C) and right gastroepiploic vein (Option D) drain the greater curvature into the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, respectively, and are not part of the esophageal portosystemic shunt. Therefore, the left gastric vein is the key portal vessel involved
questions.learning: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to liver cirrhosis. When portal blood flow is obstructed, portosystemic anastomoses form at specific sites.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, paresthesia of both feet, and gait instability for 6 months. Examination reveals pallor, loss of vibration sense, and a positive Romberg sign. Laboratory investigations show: • Hemoglobin: 6.8 g/dL • MCV: 122 fL • Peripheral smear: macro-ovalocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils • Serum LDH: markedly elevated • Serum vitamin B12: very low He is diagnosed with severe megaloblastic anemia due to pernicious anemia and started on intramuscular hydroxocobalamin therapy. Within 48 hours of initiating treatment, the treating physician closely monitors a specific electrolyte because rapid hematopoietic recovery may precipitate a life-threatening complication. Which of the following best explains this precaution?
options: Rapid intracellular shift of potassium causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias
Sudden intracellular shift of phosphate leading to respiratory muscle paralysis
Increased renal magnesium loss precipitating refractory tetany
Acute calcium influx into regenerating erythrocytes causing prolonged QT interval
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rapid intracellular shift of potassium causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias

Treatment of severe vitamin B12 deficiency can cause rapid bone marrow recovery with brisk erythropoiesis, leading to increased cellular uptake of potassium. This may precipitate:

• Acute hypokalemia
• Cardiac arrhythmias
• Sudden death in severe cases

Therefore, serum potassium should be monitored after initiating therapy for severe megaloblastic anemia. Features of vitamin B12 deficiency:

• Macrocytic megaloblastic anemia
• Hypersegmented neutrophils
• Elevated LDH (ineffective erythropoiesis)
• Neurologic deficits:

• Loss of vibration/proprioception
• Sensory ataxia
• Positive Romberg sign

Pernicious anemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leading to intrinsic factor deficiency and impaired B12 absorption.
questions.learning: Rapid intracellular shift of potassium causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias Treatment of severe vitamin B12 deficiency can cause rapid bone marrow recovery with brisk erythropoiesis, leading to increased cellular uptake of potassium.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to bloody emesis. She had 2 episodes of vomiting bright red blood and feels lightheaded and dizzy. The patient was recently diagnosed with factitious disorder after being hospitalized multiple times for a myriad of symptoms and undergoing several invasive procedures. Physical examination shows scattered ecchymoses. Rectal examination shows maroon-colored, guaiac-positive stool. After much questioning, she admits to having ingested rat poison several days ago. Immediate treatment of this patient should include which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC)

This patient has active, life-threatening bleeding (hematemesis, melena, hemodynamic symptoms) due to ingestion of warfarin-type rat poison, which causes deficiency of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). In such situations, immediate reversal is required. PCC rapidly replaces these clotting factors and provides fast hemostasis, making it the treatment of choice in acute severe bleeding.

• Vitamin K: Essential but has a delayed onset (6–24 hours); not sufficient alone initially.
• Fresh frozen plasma: Slower, requires large volumes, risk of overload.
• Cryoprecipitate: Used for fibrinogen deficiency, not anticoagulant toxicity.
