questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A baby was brought in with complaints of intermittent feculent discharge from the umbilicus. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ileal diverticulum

The presence of feculent discharge at the umbilicus with the persistence of the vitellointestinal duct is suggestive of vitelline fistula which occurs due to an ileal diverticulum.

The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct). The next best step is the USG abdomen to diagnose if the anomaly is cystic, fibrous or fistula and its connections.

Vitello intestinal duct or omphalomesenteric duct is the connection between the yolk sac and the midgut during embryonic life, which eventually gets obliterated. The persistence of the vitellointestinal duct leads to various abnormalities depending on which part of the duct remains patent.

• Persistence of the proximal intestinal end of the duct leads to the Ileal diverticula/Meckel’s diverticula.
• Persistence of the distal end near the umbilicus leads to the umbilical polyp or sinus.
• Persistence of the distal end with mucus retention leads to the cyst, which may be associated with the intestine or the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
• A fully patent vitellointestinal duct can lead to an enterocutaneous fistula.

Patent urachus occurs due to the failure of urachus to obliterate, resulting in a connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

Urachal cyst occurs when the urachus fails to obliterate but there is no connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

The image below shows a urachal cyst (UC) attached to Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) on one side and a urinary bladder (UB) on the other side with a patent tract- urachus (U).
questions.learning: Ileal diverticulum — The presence of feculent discharge at the umbilicus with the persistence of the vitellointestinal duct is suggestive of vitelline fistula which occurs due to an ileal diverticulum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 5 year old boy was suffering from low grade fever, inspiratory stridor and barking cough for past 5 days. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parainfluenza

Barking cough is a feature of laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The X-ray finding is the 'Steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months-6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever.

Management:

• Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to the rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.
• Dexamethasone-by the least invasive route (Oral>IV>IM ). It is indicated in all the grades of croup.
• Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

Antibiotics are not indicated in laryngotracheobronchitis.
questions.learning: Parainfluenza Barking cough is a feature of laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The X-ray finding is the 'Steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old G3P2L2 woman with a past history of Caesarean section and a Dilatation and curettage , presents to the ER with hypotension, tachycardia, and severe abdominal pain. On examination, fetal parts are palpable in the abdomen and Fetal heart rate is weak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

The diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture.

Previous cesarean section and Dilatation and curettage are both potential risk factors for scar dehiscence and uterine rupture. Hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, confusion, abdominal pain, scar site tenderness are all the signs of uterine rupture. Rarely, Hemoperitoneum can irritate the diaphragm and cause chest and shoulder tip pain.

CTG in uterine rupture will show non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate which might progress to late decelerations and bradycardia.

Differential diagnoses for uterine rupture:

* Pre-eclampsia

* Eclampsia

* Pulmonary embolism - amniotic fluid embolism / venous embolism

* Abruptio placenta

* Anaphylaxis to anesthesia

* Peripartum cardiomyopathy

Management of uterine rupture:

* confirm the fetal station and arrest of labor

* Stabilize the patient's vitals

* Immediate cesarean section should be performed, immediately/ as early as possible to avoid neurological or hypoxic sequelae in newborns.

* Depending on the extent of rupture and vitals on the table decision of uterine suturing or hysterectomy or sub-total hysterectomy may be taken.
questions.learning: Uterine rupture — The diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture. Previous cesarean section and Dilatation and curettage are both potential risk factors for scar dehiscence and uterine rupture.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The life expectancy at birth for a country A is 64 years. The minimum and maximum values of life expectancy are 20 years and 86 years respectively. As part of Human Development Index (HDI), what is the Life Expectancy Index for the country A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 0.667

The Human Development Index (HDI) is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and measures a country’s development based on health, education, and standard of living.

The Life Expectancy Index (LEI) is calculated using the formula:

Life Expectancy Index = (Actual life expectancy − Minimum value) / (Maximum value − Minimum value)

• Life expectancy at birth = 64 years
• Minimum value = 20 years
• Maximum value = 86 years

LEI = (64 − 20) / (86 − 20) = 44 / 66 = 0.667
questions.learning: 0.667 The Human Development Index (HDI) is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and measures a country’s development based on health, education, and standard of living.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a generalized seizure following a high-grade fever. Which of the following is the first-line drug of choice for seizure control in this acute febrile episode?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diazepam

Acute management of febrile seizures focuses on rapid termination of the seizure using benzodiazepines as first-line therapy.

• Diazepam (IV/rectal) or lorazepam (IV) are first-line drugs for ongoing seizures
• They act by enhancing GABA activity → rapid seizure control
• Most febrile seizures are self-limiting, but if seizure persists >5 minutes, treatment is required

Clinical approach:

• Ensure airway, breathing, circulation first
• Give benzodiazepine if seizure is prolonged
• Long-term antiepileptic therapy is not indicated for simple febrile seizures

Why other options are incorrect:

• Valproate and fosphenytoin are second-line agents if seizures persist
• Antibiotics have no role unless infection is specifically indicated

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A girl presents with prolonged menstrual bleeding and her investigations showed- normal platelet count, PT, and aPTT while bleeding time was increased. On further analysis, a deficiency of GpIIb-IIIa was found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glanzman thrombasthenia

The clinical vignette is suggestive of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

* Autosomal recessive platelet surface receptor disorder of GPIIb/IIIa (ITG αIIbβ3), either qualitative or quantitative - Faulty platelet aggregation and diminished clot retraction.

* Acquired GT is seen with platelet transfusions, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndrome, hairy cell leukemia, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

* Normal platelet morphology and normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, absent or decreased clot retraction, and normal platelet aggregation in the presence of ristocetin.

* Platelet aggregation is absent in the presence of epinephrine, collagen, arachidonic acid, ADP.

* Under flow cytometric analysis, CD41 and CD61 levels are markedly decreased or absent

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT part of AMTSL?

AMTSL : Active Management of Third Stage of Labour
options: Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction
Administration of oxytocin after shoulder delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bimanual compression

Bimanual compression is not part of AMTSL.

AMTSL is recommended by the WHO to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Uterotonics are the most important components in AMTSL to do so.

1.
Injecting uterotonics within 1 minute of delivery of the baby or immediately after delivery of the anterior shoulder (Option D)
Most important step
Oxytocin 10 IU im/iv infusion is the preferred uterotonic.
(Not recommended by WHO- carboprost)

2.
Delayed cord clamping

• Done within 1-3 mins of delivery
• 80 ml of additional blood goes to the fetus
• Prevents fetal anemia

3.
Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction: Modified Brandt Andrews technique (Option B)

• The uterus is pushed upwards and backward
• The traction of cord is downwards and forwards

4.
Intermittent assessment of uterine tone
Done every 15 mins for 2 hours

Note: Uterine massage or fundal massage is not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have already received prophylactic uterotonics such as oxytocin (core component of AMTSL). Hence, it is now an optional component of AMTSL that is done in patients with uterine atony as a part of the management of PPH.  (Option A)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ultrasound finding of a 24-year-old primi with 3 months of amenorrhoea is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellen's chart at 60m distance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5

The angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellens chart at 60m distance is 5 minutes.

Visual acuity is a measure of the spatial resolution of the eye or an estimation of its ability to discriminate between two points. Snellens chart is used for Visual acuity assesment.

In snellens chart the alphabets decrease in size as we move from above-downwards and these lines, from above-downwards should be read at 60, 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6, 5 and 4 m respectively. At these distances, the respective letters subtend a visual angle of 5 minutes. Hence, the largest alphabet that should be read at 60 m subtends a visual angle of 5 minutes in the eye.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the outpatient department with irritability, poor academic performance, and a history of recurrent ear infections. Otoscopic examination reveals a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid visible behind it, without any blood clot in the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The findings of a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid accumulation in the absence of acute inflammatory signs like purulence or a bulging membrane are characteristic of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as "glue ear". This condition is common in school-aged children and often results from Eustachian tube dysfunction, frequently caused by adenoid hyperplasia. Acute otitis media (Option A) would present with sudden ear pain, fever, and a red, bulging membrane. Otitis externa (Option B) involves infection of the outer ear canal, typically causing pain when the tragus is moved. Cholesteatoma (Option D) involves a keratinizing epithelial growth in the middle ear, often presenting with foul discharge and a retraction pocket. Thus, the clinical picture specifically describes non-purulent middle ear effusion. ОРТНALMOLOGY
questions.learning: The findings of a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid accumulation in the absence of acute inflammatory signs like purulence or a bulging membrane are characteristic of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as "glue ear".

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: After consuming three cones of ice cream, a man notices that his ear feels colder than the central part of his body. Which area of the brain regulates body temperature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the body temperature.

The hypothalamus is the thermoregulatory centre of the body. It acts as a central command centre for thermoregulation, ensuring that the body maintains a relatively constant core temperature despite external temperature fluctuations.

* The reflex responses triggered by cold originate from the posterior hypothalamus,

* The reflex responses initiated by warmth primarily stem from the anterior hypothalamus.

Activation of the anterior hypothalamus leads to cutaneous vasodilation and sweating, while lesions in this area can result in hyperthermia, with rectal temperatures sometimes rising to 43°C (109.4°F).

Stimulation of the posterior hypothalamus induces shivering, and animals with lesions in this region experience a decrease in body temperature toward that of the surrounding environment.
questions.learning: Hypothalamus — The hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the body temperature. The hypothalamus is the thermoregulatory centre of the body.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the control of enzyme activity by phosphorylation or dephosphorylation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Covalent modification

The control of enzyme activity by phosphorylation or dephosphorylation is best explained by covalent modification.

Covalent modification is a key regulatory mechanism in which enzymes or proteins undergo chemical changes through the addition or removal of functional groups, altering their activity, stability, or interactions. One of the most common types is phosphorylation, where a phosphate group is added to a protein, typically by a kinase, leading to activation or inhibition of the target enzyme.

Conversely, dephosphorylation, catalyzed by phosphatases, removes the phosphate group, reversing the effect. This dynamic process plays a crucial role in cell signalling, metabolism, and gene regulation. For example, in glycogen metabolism, glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation to promote glycogen breakdown, while glycogen synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation to stop glycogen synthesis. These modifications ensure rapid and reversible control of cellular functions in response to physiological needs.

A few enzyme covalent modifications that regulate enzyme kinetics include:

* Partial proteolysis

* Acetylation

* Methylation

* ADP-ribosylation

* Phosphorylation

Other options:

Option A: Competitive inhibition is a type of inhibition that occurs when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the same site that the substrate would normally occupy. It, therefore, competes with the substrate for binding to the enzyme active site. The effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the concentration of the substrate. Km is increased, but Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition.

Option B: Allosteric inhibition occurs when a molecule binds to a site on an enzyme other than the active site, causing a conformational change that reduces the enzyme's activity. This regulatory mechanism is crucial for feedback control in metabolic pathways.

Option C: Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

* Non-Competitive inhibitors

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the upper limit of Medical Termination of Pregnancy , according to the MTP Act of 2021?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 24 weeks

The upper limit of MTP is 24 weeks.

The opinion of one doctor is sufficient for abortions up to 20 weeks. For abortions from 20-24 weeks, the opinions of 2 doctors are required.

Medical termination of pregnancy is legal in India for therapeutic, eugenic, humanitarian, and eugenic reasons. It should be conducted only by registered medical practitioners in government hospitals, or other private hospitals that are recognized by the government. The registered medical practitioner should have assisted in conducting 25 cases of medical termination of pregnancy in a recognized hospital. If a person or hospital goes against this rule, they are liable to be punished rigorously for a period of 2 years, which may extend to 7 years.

Pearl PF1107: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act 1971

Indications :

* Therapeutic : When continuation of pregnancy endangers the life of the woman, or may injure her physical or mental health.

* Eugenic : The risk of child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality. This includes first trimester viral infections, maternal drug intake (thalidomide, cortisone, antimitotics), xray or radioisotope treatment of the mother, insanity of parents and viral hepatitis.

* Humanitarian : Pregnancy resulted from rape.

* Social : Pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives.

Rules :

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government recognised hospital.

* Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is a minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband is not necessary.

* If the woman is not willing, abortion can not be performed on the request of the husband alone.

* The woman need not produce proof of her age. The statement of the woman that she is over 18 years of age is accepted.

* It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

* Professional secrecy has to be maintained.

* If the period of pregnancy is below 20 weeks, it can be terminated on the opinion of a single doctor.

* If the period of pregnancy is between 20-24 weeks, two doctors must opine that there is an indication. Once there is an indication, the termination can be done by any one doctor.

* In an emergency, the termination can be done by a single doctor, even without the required training, even after 20 weeks, without consulting a second doctor, in a private hospital which is not recognised.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Confidentiality :

The head of the hospital must maintain a register for recording the details of MTP. This register is a secret document which should be kept under safe custody for five years, and each patient is given a reference number. The name of the patient should not be entered anywhere, any case sheet or operation theatre register or any other record.
questions.learning: 24 weeks The upper limit of MTP is 24 weeks. The opinion of one doctor is sufficient for abortions up to 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain and redness in the right eye after sustaining an injury while welding. On examination, the finding shown in the image below is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes a classic corneal foreign body, a common occupational injury among welders and metalworkers. The accompanying image shows a metallic fragment embedded in the superficial corneal layers. The immediate management involves the removal of the foreign body to prevent infection and promote healing. This is typically performed at the slit lamp using a sterile 26-gauge needle or a specialized ophthalmic burr after applying topical anesthesia. If a "rust ring" has formed around the metallic site, as is common with iron-based fragments, it must also be carefully debrided. Steroids (Option A) are generally avoided initially as they can delay epithelial healing and mask infection. Surgical exploration (Option B) is reserved for suspected globe perforations, which are not indicated by this superficial presentation. Keratoplasty (Option C), or corneal transplant, is a radical procedure for end-stage corneal disease and is not an initial treatment for a foreign body. Following removal, a topical antibiotic ointment and sometimes a patch or bandage contact lens are prescribed

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea not responding to antibiotics. On examination, granulation tissue is seen in EAC, facial nerve palsy was present. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, and granulation tissue in EAC and facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease.

*

Treatment:

(i) Diabetic control.

(ii) Ear toileting

(iii) Antibiotic treatment against the causative organism(P. aeruginosa) for 6–8 weeks or more.

*

Antibiotics found effective are:

*

Gentamicin combined with ticarcillin. (intravenous)

*

Third-generation cephalosporins combined with an aminoglycoside. (intravenous)

*

Quinolones combined with rifampin. (oral)

If patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.

Prolonged antibiotic treatment has replaced radical surgery and resections done earlier for this condition.
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, and granulation tissue in EAC and facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: To study the dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, which sampling method would be most appropriate for obtaining a representative sample?
questions.explanation: To study dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, the population is highly heterogeneous with variations in income, education, occupation, culture, and locality. To ensure proper representation of all these subgroups, stratified random sampling is the most appropriate method. In this method, the population is divided into homogeneous strata (e.g., income groups, regions, age groups), and then random samples are taken from each stratum. This ensures that all important sections of the population are proportionally represented, leading to more accurate and reliable results. Why Other Options Are Less Suitable (A) Cluster sampling: May miss diversity if clusters are not representative (C) Simple random sampling: May underrepresent key subgroups (D) Systematic sampling: Can introduce bias if there is hidden pattern in population
questions.learning: To study dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, the population is highly heterogeneous with variations in income, education, occupation, culture, and locality.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Can you identify the particular type of movement taking place in the intestinal tract?
questions.explanation: The image depicts peristalsis, which is the primary propulsive movement of the gastrointestinal tract. Peristalsis involves a coordinated wave of smooth muscle contraction preceded by a wave of relaxation. Specifically, the circular muscles contract behind the food bolus while the longitudinal muscles relax, effectively squeezing the contents forward toward the anus. Segmented movement (Option A) involves localized, rhythmic contractions that mix food with digestive juices but do not provide significant forward propulsion. Intersegmental contraction (Option C) is not a standard physiological term for these movements. Diffusion (Option D) is a microscopic transport process for individual molecules rather than a macroscopic mechanical movement of the gut. Peristalsis is regulated by the myenteric plexus of the enteric nervous system and is enhanced by distension of the gut wall. It is essential for moving the bolus through the esophagus, stomach, and intestines for efficient digestion and excretion
questions.learning: The image depicts peristalsis, which is the primary propulsive movement of the gastrointestinal tract. Peristalsis involves a coordinated wave of smooth muscle contraction preceded by a wave of relaxation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 13-year-old male presents to the OPD with severe pain in the right testis after being hit by a cricket ball 2 hours ago. On examination, there is severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Surgical exploration

The given clinical vignette of severe pain in the right testis along with a negative cremasteric reflex is highly suggestive of testicular torsion.  It is a surgical emergency, and if left untreated, the testes may become gangrenous. Early surgery undertaken to untwist the testis gives a better outcome.

Testicular torsion is the twisting of the spermatic cord and its contents such that the testicular blood supply becomes compromised.

Etiology and risk factors-

* High investment of the tunica vaginalis(like a clapper in a bell). Most common cause.

* Inversion of the testis.

* Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis.

Clinical features of testicular torsion are - scrotal pain and swelling, erythema, negative cremasteric reflex, nausea, and vomiting, the testis seems high in the scrotum and the twisted cord can sometimes be palpated.

* Prehn’s Sign is used to differentiate the torsion of testis from acute epididymo orchitis. In the case of acute epididymo orchitis, the pain gets relieved on the elevation of the testis but not in torsion of testes.

* Deming’s sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle and the cord twisting cause the affected testis to be positioned higher in torsion testes.

Even though Doppler ultrasound scanning can confrm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis, false-positive results are commonly seen, hence it is not routinely recommended.

Urgent scrotal exploration in case of doubtful diagnosis.  A transverse scrotal incision is taken. If the testis is viable, twisting is prevented by fixation with three non-absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe.

If the testis is infarcted after the cord is untwisted, an orchidectomy must be undertaken and the opposite testis must be fixed to the scrotum to preserve fertility and prevent torsion. If the affected testis is viable after the cord is untwisted, both the affected and the contralateral testes are fixed to the scrotum (bilateral orchiopexy) using non-absorbable sutures.

Other options:

Option A and D: The optimal timeframe for surgical intervention and testicular salvage is within 6 hours from the onset of pain. Hence, seeking early urological consultation at presentation is essential, even if confirmatory tests are not yet available.

Option B: Ultrasound guided arterial doppler has to be taken, not venous. Also even for USG arterial doppler false positives are commonly seen.
questions.learning: Surgical exploration — The given clinical vignette of severe pain in the right testis along with a negative cremasteric reflex is highly suggestive of testicular torsion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: miRNA binds to which part of the mRNA to inhibit translation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3' UTR

Micro-RNA (miRNA) is an endogenous non-coding RNA that typically binds to the 3’-untranslated regions (UTRs) of target messenger-RNAs (mRNAs). The primary function of miRNA is to modulate the translation of target mRNAs into their corresponding proteins. After the target RNA is transcribed from its gene (post-transcriptional), the miRNA may either induce mRNA cleavage or repress its translation. This is referred to as post-transcriptional gene silencing or RNA interference.

RNA interference(RNAi) is a biological process in which miRNA or siRNA molecules inhibit gene expression by neutralizing targeted mRNAs.The microRNA (miRNA) belongs to a group of non-coding genes. The miRNA genes are transcribed but not translated into proteins. They play a role in the regulation of the expression of the target gene by post-transcriptional silencing.

Mechanism:

• The miRNA gene present in the nucleus is transcribed to primary miRNA, which is further converted to pre-miRNA by an enzyme DROSHA intranuclearly and exported to the cytoplasm by an export protein called Exportin 5.
• The pre-miRNA undergoes trimming, by an enzyme called DICER, into mature single-stranded miRNA.
• The mature miRNA is associated with a multiprotein aggregate called RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
• The target mRNAs contain seed sequences in their 3′ untranslated region (UTR) that determines the specificity of miRNA binding and gene silencing.

Depending on the base pairing between the miRNA strand and its target mRNA, the RISC causes gene silencing either by mRNA cleavage (degradation or deadenylation) or by repressing its translation.

siRNA is similar in function to miRNA and is used in RNA interference.

miRNA expression has been found to be dysregulated in many cancers. Such misregulation is thought to have a causal role in the pathogenesis of such cancers. Some types of miRNAs are oncogenic (referred to as oncomiRs) and are overexpressed in cancerous tissue. On the other hand, tumor-suppressive miRNAs that counteract oncogenic characteristics are found to be underexpressed in cancers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following chart shows the hormonal variations in the menstrual cycle. Identify the true statement : (LH: luteinizing hormone, FSH: follicle-stimulating hormone)
options: The blue line represents FSH hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The blue line represents FSH hormone

The blue line represents follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle.

Other options :

* The pink line represents luteinizing hormone.

* The grey line represents estrogen.

* The purple line represents progesterone.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.

* Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)

* Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22.

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

* Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).

* Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Progesterone levels are high.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.

* Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

Pearl PF0568: Hormonal Regulation of Menstrual Cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following connective tissue degradation disorder is associated with aortic aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marfan's Syndrome

Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, leading to defective elastic fiber formation in connective tissues. Weakness of the aortic media predisposes to aortic root dilatation, aneurysm, and dissection, which is a major cause of mortality in these patients.

It is also characterized by tall stature, long limbs (arachnodactyly), lens dislocation, and skeletal abnormalities.

Why not other options:

• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Defect in collagen synthesis causing hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility; vascular complications may occur in rare types but aortic aneurysm classically associated with Marfan syndrome.
• Atherosclerosis: Causes arterial narrowing and plaque formation, not primarily a connective-tissue degradation disorder.
• Scurvy: Vitamin C deficiency causing defective collagen synthesis leading to bleeding gums and poor wound healing, not aortic aneurysm.
questions.learning: Marfan's Syndrome Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, leading to defective elastic fiber formation in connective tissues.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to standard biomedical waste management color coding, into which colored bag should used cotton swabs be disposed of?
questions.explanation: Bio-medical waste must be segregated at the point of generation to ensure safe disposal and prevent infections. According to current Indian guidelines, the Yellow bag is designated for highly infectious non-plastic waste. This includes anatomical waste, soiled bedding, and materials contaminated with blood or body fluids, such as used cotton swabs, bandages, and gauze. The Red bag (Option B) is for recyclable plastic waste like syringes (without needles) and IV tubes. The Blue bag (Option C) or puncture-proof container is for glassware and metallic implants. Transparent or white containers are for sharps. Because used cotton swabs are highly porous and soak up biological fluids, they carry a high risk of pathogen transmission and must be destroyed through high-temperature incineration or deep burial, for which the yellow bag is the mandatory category. Proper adherence to this color coding is a critical responsibility of all healthcare personnel to maintain hospital hygiene and community safety
questions.learning: Bio-medical waste must be segregated at the point of generation to ensure safe disposal and prevent infections. According to current Indian guidelines, the Yellow bag is designated for highly infectious non-plastic waste.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with features suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. Microscopic examination reveals gram- positive cocci arranged in chains. What is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation: Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a non-suppurative inflammatory complication that occurs 2-4 weeks after a pharyngeal infection. The specific etiological agent responsible for triggering this autoimmune response is Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS). Microscopically, these are characterized as gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Streptococcus viridans (Option A) is a common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis but does not trigger ARF. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) causes pneumonia and meningitis and typically appears as gram-positive diplococci. Enterococcus (Option D) is associated with urinary tract and abdominal infections. ARF results from molecular mimicry between the streptococcal M-protein and human heart tissue. Diagnosis is made clinically using the Jones Criteria. Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is required for these patients to prevent recurrent attacks and subsequent chronic rheumatic heart disease

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery develops sudden hemodynamic instability after a failed attempt at subclavian vein catheterization. On examination, the trachea is deviated to one side and breath sounds are absent on the same side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of sudden hemodynamic instability following a failed subclavian vein catheterization is highly indicative of a tension pneumothorax. This life-threatening condition occurs when a "one-way valve" effect allows air into the pleural space but prevents its escape, leading to rapidly increasing intrathoracic pressure. Key diagnostic signs found on examination include tracheal deviation away from the affected side and a complete absence of breath sounds on the side of the injury. Bronchospasm (Option A) presents with wheezing but does not cause tracheal shift. Pulmonary embolism (Option C) causes hypoxia and tachycardia but typically leaves the trachea midline and breath sounds intact. Aspiration pneumonitis (Option D) causes respiratory distress and crackles rather than an acute lung collapse with mediastinal shift. Therefore, the combination of a procedural complication, shifted trachea, and absent breath sounds confirms tension pneumothorax as the primary diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of sudden hemodynamic instability following a failed subclavian vein catheterization is highly indicative of a tension pneumothorax.

The slide shows the histopathology of Hashimoto thyroiditis, with:

• Follicular destruction
• Reduced colloid with increased interstitial connective tissue
• Small lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration
• A well-developed germinal centre may be seen
• Hurthle (Askanazy) cells that have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm lining the follicles

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is also known as struma lymphomatosa or lymphocytic thyroiditis. It is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure.

Clinical features:

• Most prevalent between 45-65 years of age
• More common in females
• Painless enlargement of the thyroid
• Hashitoxicosis: When the auto-antibodies attack and damage the follicles, there is a sudden release of thyroid hormones from these follicles. This leads to a transient phase of thyrotoxicosis.
• Hypothyroidism: Since the follicles are damaged and cannot form the hormones anymore, these patients tend to be in a state of hypothyroidism.

Diagnosis:

• T3 and T4 are low
• TSH is raised
• Autoantibodies against:

• Thyroid receptors
• Thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
• Thyroglobulin

These patients are managed with thyroid hormone replacement therapy.

In patients with long-standing goiter, there is a risk of compressive features and the development of thyroid lymphoma. Such cases can be treated with total thyroidectomy. It may also predispose to papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Histological features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include polygonal to spindle-shaped cells in the form of nests, trabeculae or follicles. Small, round anaplastic cells may be found in some cases and amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma.

The given slide below shows medullary carcinoma of thyroid:

Option C: Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by hyperthyroidism due to circulating autoantibodies. The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to the TSH receptors, causing overgrowth of the thyroid gland and increased thyroid hormone synthesis. Histologically, there is acinar cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia with the absence of normal colloid in the tall columnar epithelium (normally the epithelium is flat with colloid). Lymphoid infiltrates, consisting predominantly of T cells, along with scattered B cells and mature plasma cells, are present throughout the interstitium. Germinal centers are common.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the American Heart Association (AHA), what is the 6th link added to the chain of survival?
questions.explanation: The American Heart Association (AHA) expanded the Chain of Survival concept by adding a sixth link: recovery and rehabilitation. This addition reflects the growing recognition that survival extends far beyond the immediate resuscitation period. The complete AHA Chain of Survival now includes early recognition and activation of emergency response, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, post-cardiac arrest care, and finally, recovery and rehabilitation. Rapid defibrillation (Option A) is already included as the critical third link. High-quality CPR (Option C) constitutes the second link, emphasizing proper depth and rate. Advanced airway management (Option D) is part of the fourth link (advanced life support) but should never interfere with or delay chest compressions and defibrillation. Therefore, the newly introduced sixth link acknowledges the long-term support needed for survivors
questions.learning: The American Heart Association (AHA) expanded the Chain of Survival concept by adding a sixth link: recovery and rehabilitation. This addition reflects the growing recognition that survival extends far beyond the immediate resuscitation period.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Obliteration of right cardiac border on chest X-Ray indicates pathology involving which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right middle lobe

Right middle lobe pathology causes obliteration of right cardiac border.

The silhouette sign is the loss of clear demarcation between normal lung and soft tissue (e.g., heart, diaphragm). This occurs when the lung parenchyma is no longer filled with air and the contrast between air and soft tissue is lost.

A silhouette in a chest radiograph is the outline of a particular structure that is formed at the interface of two tissues with different tissue densities eg. cardiac silhouette between the heart and the lung. Blurring/obliteration of these normal silhouettes due to disease pathologies is known as the silhouette sign.

The silhouette can be obscured only by a pathology that is in direct anatomical contact, eg. right cardiac border will be obscured when there is right middle lobe pneumonia. Hence, the silhouette sign helps us in localizing the site of pathology.

Given below is a list of normal silhouettes on chest radiographs as seen on the PA view. Loss of these silhouettes are indicative of the site of pathology:

Obliterated silhouette
Site of pathology

Right para-tracheal stripe
Right upper lobe

Right heart border
Right middle lobe or
medial right lower lobe

Right hemidiaphragm
Right lower lobe

Aortic knuckle
Left upper lobe
(posterior segment)

Left heart border
Lingula segments of
left upper lobe

Left hemidiaphragm
or descending aorta
Left lower lobe

The left image is a normal chest radiograph with the red line indicating the silhouette of the right heart border and right middle lobe.

The right image shows the same red line delineating where the silhouette should be, but is lost due to consolidation in the right middle lobe.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the most abundant plasma protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Albumin

Albumin is the most abundant protein in the blood and accounts for about 50% of all plasma proteins.

Serum protein electrophoresis is a method of separation and identification of proteins based on their net charge, size, and shape. The largest peak that lies closest to the positive electrode (left corner) is that of albumin since it is present in the largest proportion in the plasma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: During the examination of a patient with a suspected right forearm fracture, the patient is asked to make a fist. A characteristic change in finger alignment is observed. What is the name of this clinical sign?
questions.explanation: The image shows the index finger remaining extended while the other fingers are flexed into a fist. This is the classic Pointing Index Sign, also called the "Index finger sign" seen in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) palsy — a branch of the median nerve. AIN injury causes paralysis of FDP to index finger and FPL, so when making a fist, the index finger cannot flex at the DIP joint and remains pointing straight out. This is commonly associated with supracondylar fractures or forearm fractures compressing the AIN. Why Other Options are Wrong: (A) Froment's Sign : Tests ulnar nerve integrity; patient cannot pinch paper between thumb and index finger without flexing the thumb IP joint (FPL compensation). No index pointing involved. (C) Benediction Sign : Also a median nerve palsy sign but seen at rest, where index and middle fingers remain extended due to FDS/FDP weakness. Different nerve level injury. (D) Policeman Tip Deformity : Associated with Erb's palsy (C5-C6 brachial plexus injury), showing shoulder adduction, internal rotation, and elbow extension : an entirely different deformity
questions.learning: The image shows the index finger remaining extended while the other fingers are flexed into a fist. This is the classic Pointing Index Sign, also called the "Index finger sign" seen in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) palsy — a branch of the median nerve.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A disease with mitochondrial inheritance is inherited from which family member?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial inheritance follows a strict maternal pattern because mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the egg. During fertilization, the sperm contributes its nuclear DNA but its mitochondria are typically degraded or excluded, meaning only the mother passes mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) to her offspring. Consequently, an affected mother will pass the trait to all of her children, while an affected father (Option C) will not pass it to any of his offspring. Option B (paternal grandmother) is incorrect as paternal lineages do not transmit mtDNA. Option D is incorrect because inheritance is uniparental. Classic examples of mitochondrial disorders include Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) and MELAS syndrome. These diseases often exhibit variable expression due to heteroplasmy, where a cell contains a mix of both normal and mutated mtDNA. Therefore, the maternal line is the only source of transmission for these specific genetic conditions

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-week primigravida c/o reduced vision at night. She has been avoiding papaya, mango, and other fruits throughout her pregnancy as she thinks they could be abortifacients. It is the primary duty of which of the following workers to provide counseling and information to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ASHA

Amongst the given options, it is the duty of the ASHA to provide counseling and information to this pregnant patient

An ASHA is a trained female community health activist and a resident woman of the village with a formal education of at least up to 10th grade. She should preferably be in the age group of 25 to 45 years (married/divorced/widow) and have qualities such as good communication skills and leadership skills. The general norm of selection recommends having one ASHA for 1000 population, but in tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm could be relaxed to one ASHA per habitation.

Roles of ASHA:

• To create awareness and provide information to the community on determinants of health such as nutrition, basic sanitation, and hygienic practices
• To counsel women on birth preparedness, the importance of safe delivery, breast-feeding and complementary feeding, immunization, and contraception
• To counsel women on the prevention of common infections including reproductive tract infection/sexually transmitted infection
• To mobilize the community and help them in accessing health and health-related services.
• To arrange and escort pregnant women and children requiring treatment/admission to the nearest pre-identified health facility
• To inform sub-center/primary health center about the births and deaths in her village and any unusual health problems/disease outbreaks in the community
• To promote the construction of household toilets under the total sanitation campaign

Other Options:

Option A (ANM): An Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) is a trained health worker who provides basic healthcare services, including antenatal care, delivery, and postnatal care. Although an ANM can provide counseling and information to pregnant women, the primary responsibility for this role lies with the ASHA worker.

Option B (AWW): An Anganwadi Worker (AWW) is responsible for providing basic health care, nutrition, and preschool education to children under the age of six, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. While AWWs play a vital role in maternal and child health, counseling pregnant women on health-related issues is not their primary responsibility.

Option C (Trained birth attendant): A trained birth attendant is responsible for assisting with childbirth and providing postpartum care. Although they may provide some counseling and information, this role is primarily focused on the delivery process rather than ongoing counseling throughout pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with ptosis and muscle weakness that worsens by evening and improves after rest in the morning. His symptoms show improvement following administration of neostigmine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to "fatigable" muscle weakness, meaning the weakness worsens with repetitive use or as the day progresses (diurnal variation). Ptosis and diplopia (ocular myasthenia) are the most common presenting symptoms. The hallmark of MG is the clinical improvement of symptoms with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine or edrophonium (Tensilon test). These drugs increase the availability of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, briefly overcoming the receptor blockade. Huntington chorea (Option B) is a genetic disorder presenting with choreiform movements and cognitive decline. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS, Option C) involves progressive upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, causing permanent, non-fatigable weakness and atrophy. External ophthalmoplegia (Option D) refers to restricted eye movements but is a descriptive term, not a primary diagnosis, and would not respond to neostigmine. Thus, the classic presentation of fatigable ptosis responsive to anticholinesterases confirms Myasthenia Gravis
questions.learning: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure(s) in the following histological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glomerulus

The above histology image shows the glomerulus.

Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium. Blood enters the tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves it through an efferent arteriole. It is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitial connective between seminiferous tubules.

The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue in between. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which produce spermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function.

The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round, or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamy appearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.

The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells.

Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells:

• α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon
• β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin
• δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans.

Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyaline mass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known.

The image given below shows Hassall's corpuscle.
questions.learning: Glomerulus — The above histology image shows the glomerulus. Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is found to be HBsAg positive with high HBV DNA levels on routine antenatal screening. She has no clinical features of liver failure. What is the most appropriate management during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir

Pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B infection and high HBV DNA levels (>200,000 IU/mL) should receive tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) during the third trimester (typically from 28–32 weeks of gestation) to reduce the risk of mother-to-child (vertical) transmission. Tenofovir is the preferred antiviral in pregnancy because of its efficacy and favorable safety profile.

• Neonatal prophylaxis: Hepatitis B vaccine + Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth is essential to further reduce vertical transmission.
• Breastfeeding: Permitted after appropriate neonatal immunoprophylaxis; tenofovir is considered compatible with breastfeeding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pegylated interferon: Contraindicated in pregnancy due to its antiproliferative and teratogenic effects.
• C. Zidovudine: Used for HIV, not for prevention of HBV transmission.
• D. Acyclovir: Active against HSV and VZV; it has no role in the management of chronic hepatitis B.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of Brown Sequard syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Complete transection of spinal cord

Complete transection of the spinal cord is not a feature of Brown Sequard syndrome.

Brown sequard syndrome occurs due to transection of the spinal cord only on one side. This results in blocking of all motor functions on the side of the transection in all segments below the transection level.

Features include:

• Ipsilateral weakness - due to corticospinal tract
• Ipsilateral loss of joint position and vibration sensation - due to posterior column
• Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation - due to the spinothalamic tract involvement
• Unilateral radicular pain
• Muscle atrophy or loss of deep tendon reflex may be present

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding the instrument shown below?
options: It is used for termination of pregnancy up to 12 weeks
Can be done on an OP basis
The capacity of the syringe is 30 ml
It creates a negative pressure of 660 mmHg
questions.explanation: The instrument depicted is the Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) syringe, a widely used tool for uterine evacuation. Statement C is "not true" because a standard double-valve MVA syringe typically has a capacity of 60 ml, not 30 ml. MVA is highly effective for the surgical termination of pregnancy up to 12 weeks of gestation (Option A) and for managing incomplete miscarriages. One of its primary advantages is that it can be safely performed on an outpatient (OP) basis under local anesthesia (Option B), reducing the need for general anesthesia and hospital stay. The syringe is designed to create a consistent negative pressure of approximately 660 mmHg (or 26 inches of Hg) when the plunger is withdrawn and the valves are released (Option D). This pressure is sufficient to evacuate the uterine contents effectively while minimizing trauma to the endometrial lining. Understanding the mechanical specifications and clinical indications for MVA is fundamental for providers managing early pregnancy complications
questions.learning: The instrument depicted is the Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) syringe, a widely used tool for uterine evacuation. Statement C is "not true" because a standard double-valve MVA syringe typically has a capacity of 60 ml, not 30 ml.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following scenarios can outlet forceps be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Head at perineum

Outlet forceps can be used when the head of the fetus is at the perineum.

Outlet forceps/ Wrigley's forceps is light, about a third of the weight of ordinary long-curved forceps. The instrument is short which is due to a reduction in the length of the shanks and handles. It has a marked cephalic curve with a slight pelvic curve.

Criteria for outlet forceps delivery:

* Scalp at introitus without separating labia

* Skull at the pelvic floor

* Sagittal suture in anterioposterior diameter, right or left occiput anterior, occiput anterior

* Fetal head on the perineum

* Rotation less than 45 degrees

The image below shows Wrigley's forceps/outlet forceps:

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.
questions.learning: Head at perineum Outlet forceps can be used when the head of the fetus is at the perineum. Outlet forceps/ Wrigley's forceps is light, about a third of the weight of ordinary long-curved forceps.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A blood spill in the operation theatre must be cleaned with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlorine compound

Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.

If the spill contains large amounts of blood or body fluids, clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard the contaminated materials in appropriate, labelled containment.

A 1:10–1:100 dilution of 5.25%–6.15% sodium hypochlorite (i.e., household bleach) or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant has been recommended for decontaminating blood spills.
questions.learning: Chlorine compound Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient engages in strenuous exercise, skips a meal, and later consumes alcohol at a party. Alcohol intake inhibits which biochemical process, thereby increasing the risk of developing hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase produces an excess of NADH, significantly increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver. This high ratio shifts metabolic reactions away from glucose production by preventing the conversion of lactate to pyruvate and malate to oxaloacetate, both of which are essential substrates for gluconeogenesis. Hypoglycemia occurs because the body cannot synthesize new glucose once glycogen stores are depleted (common after exercise or fasting). Alcohol does not directly inhibit glycogenolysis (Option B), but it becomes the primary issue when glycogen is already gone. The HMP shunt (Option C) and ketone body formation (Option D) are not the primary pathways responsible for blood glucose maintenance. In fact, alcohol metabolism can actually promote ketogenesis. Therefore, the inhibition of gluconeogenesis is the specific mechanism behind alcohol-induced fasting hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Alcohol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase produces an excess of NADH, significantly increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the online portal used for delivering mental healthcare services via telephone and other digital platforms for mental disorders such as schizophrenia, under the National Mental Health Programme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tele-manas

Tele-MANAS is the national digital mental health platform launched under the National Mental Health Programme to provide telephonic and online mental health services.

It offers 24×7 toll-free counseling, referral, and follow-up care for conditions including schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders.

| Coverage | Available across India

| Target conditions | Depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, substance abuse

| Access | Toll-free helpline

Other portals like NIKSHAY (TB), U-WIN (immunization), and Quinitin are unrelated to mental health services.

| ------ | -------

| A. NIKSHAY | Portal for tuberculosis patient management

| B. Tele-MANAS | ✔ Tele mental health services

| C. Quinitin | Not a recognized national health portal

| D. U-WIN | Digital platform for immunization tracking

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with HIV presents with diarrhoea. Stool microscopy reveals 11-12 micron oocysts with two sporocysts each. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclospora cayetanensis

The organism with oocysts of size 11-12 μm is Cyclospora cayetanensis.

Cyclospora is a coccidian parasite. The sporulated oocysts are infectious to humans. They reside in the enterocytes in the small intestine. The infection causes prolonged diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and vomiting, which is more severe in immunocompromised individuals.

On a wet mount of the faeces, oocysts are seen as red spheres when stained with acid-fast stain. Sporulated oocysts of Cyclospora are 11-12 μm in size, round, and contain 2 sporocysts, each having two sporozoites. Treatment is by giving cotrimoxazole twice daily for seven days.

Other options:

Option A: Oocysts of Cystoisospora are 23-36 μm, oval, and contain two sporocysts, each having four sporozoites. They are uniformly acid-fast.

Option B: Sporulated oocysts of Cryptosporidium are spherical, 4-5 μm in size, and acid-fast. It is implicated in causing traveller's diarrhoea and chronic persistent diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The two Cryptosporidium species responsible are Cryptosporidium hominis and Cryptosporidium parvum.

Option D: Ingestion of cysts in non-chlorinated water can contract infection from parasites such as Giardia lamblia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct with respect to antenatal USG examination? 1. It helps in detecting gross fetal anomalies. 2. It helps in identifying multiple pregnancies. 3. It helps in identifying viable pregnancy. 4. Best dating is possible with third trimester ultrasound scan. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3 only

Antenatal ultrasonography (USG) is an essential investigation in pregnancy. It is used to confirm viability, determine the number of fetuses, detect fetal anomalies, assess gestational age, placental location, and amniotic fluid volume.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. It helps in detecting gross fetal anomalies. Correct.
• 2. It helps in identifying multiple pregnancies. Correct.
• 3. It helps in identifying viable pregnancy. Correct (demonstration of fetal cardiac activity).
• 4. Best dating is possible with third trimester ultrasound scan. Incorrect. First-trimester ultrasound (CRL measurement) provides the most accurate dating of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presented to the NICU with respiratory distress and meconium discharge from the umbilicus. The condition occurs due to the patency of the which structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitellointestinal duct

The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac.

The primitive gut is connected to the definitive yolk sac through a narrow stalk-like communication known as the vitellointestinal duct. It is also known as vitelline duct or yolk stalk or omphalomesenteric duct.

Due to the folding of the embryo in the cephalocaudal and lateral directions, the embryo gets enclosed all around by ectoderm, except in the region through which the vitellointestinal duct passes. In this region, there is a circular aperture, which is now called the umbilical opening. The vitellointestinal duct completely obliterates by the 7th week of development.

Vitelline duct abnormalities:

* Meckel's diverticulum: In about 2% of the individuals, a portion of the vitelline duct persists an outpouching of the ileum called, Meckel diverticulum. The diverticulum is usually asymptomatic unless it contains heterotopic pancreatic or gastric mucosa, which may lead to bleeding, ulceration, or perforation.

* Vitelline cyst: In some individuals, both the ends of the vitelline duct transform into fibrous cords. However, the middle portion of the duct forms a large cyst called, enterocystoma, or vitelline cyst. As the fibrous cords run across the peritoneal cavity, it may lead to intestinal obstruction, strangulation, or volvulus.

* Vitelline fistula: When the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length, it forms a direct communication between the primitive gut and the umbilicus, a condition called an umbilical fistula or vitelline fistula. The newborn characteristically presents with meconium discharge from the umbilicus.
questions.learning: Vitellointestinal duct — The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent discomfort, pain, and a feeling of pressure behind her left eye. She has intermittent, reducible proptosis, with symptoms worsening when bending forward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hallmark of orbital varices is intermittent, transient proptosis (eyeball protrusion) that is triggered by maneuvers that increase venous pressure in the head and neck. Specifically, the symptoms characteristically intensify when the patient bends forward, strains (Valsalva maneuver), or coughs. Varices are low-flow venous malformations that expand under high pressure. Orbital hemangioma (Option A) is a more common orbital tumor, but it causes constant and slowly progressive proptosis rather than the posture-dependent intermittent type. Orbital metastasis (Option C) typically presents in older patients with rapid, painful proptosis and a known primary cancer. An Orbital dermoid cyst (Option D) is a slow-growing, firm, painless mass usually found at the orbital margins from birth. Diagnosis of orbital varices is confirmed by imaging, such as CT or MRI, performed while the patient is performing a Valsalva maneuver to visualize the venous dilation. Management is usually conservative unless the varices cause severe pain, vision loss from nerve compression, or significant cosmetic disfigurement
questions.learning: The hallmark of orbital varices is intermittent, transient proptosis (eyeball protrusion) that is triggered by maneuvers that increase venous pressure in the head and neck.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain, acute diarrhea, and is diagnosed with celiac disease. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
options: IgA Tissue Transglutaminase antibodies are present
IgG deamidated Gliadin antibodies are present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Associated with HLA DQ6/DQ11

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten (gliadin) in genetically predisposed individuals.

Celiac disease is strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8, not DQ6/DQ11, making that statement false. Diagnosis relies on IgA anti–tissue transglutaminase antibodies and supportive serology like IgG deamidated gliadin peptides. Histologic grading of villous atrophy is done using the Marsh classification.

| Stage | Histological Feature

| ----- | --------------------

| Marsh 0 | Normal mucosa

| Marsh 1 | ↑ Intraepithelial lymphocytes

| Marsh 2 | + Crypt hyperplasia

| Marsh 3 | Villous atrophy (partial → total)

| Antibody | Type | Use

| -------- | ---- | ---

| Anti-tTG | IgA | Best screening test

| Anti-endomysial (EMA) | IgA | Highly specific

| Deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) | IgG/IgA | IgA deficiency, children

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are indications of removal of intrauterine device? 1. Persistent irregular uterine bleeding 2. Perforation of uterus 3. Pyelonephritis 4. Pregnancy with device in situ Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

An intrauterine device (IUD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. Although it is generally safe, removal is indicated in certain situations such as:

• 1. Persistent irregular uterine bleeding ✓

• Persistent or troublesome bleeding that does not respond to medical treatment is an indication for IUD removal after excluding other causes.

• 2. Perforation of uterus ✓

• Uterine perforation is a definite indication for removal, usually by laparoscopy or laparotomy, depending on the location of the device.

• 3. Pyelonephritis ✗

• Pyelonephritis is an infection of the upper urinary tract and is not related to IUD use; therefore, it is not an indication for IUD removal.

• 4. Pregnancy with device in situ ✓

• If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in place and the strings are visible, the device should be removed early because it reduces the risk of miscarriage, septic abortion, and preterm birth.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 An intrauterine device (IUD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. Although it is generally safe, removal is indicated in certain situations such as: • 1.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with bowing of the legs, and an X-ray of the wrist shows characteristic abnormalities. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of bow legs (genu varum) combined with the classic radiological findings of metaphyseal fraying, cupping, and splaying at the wrist is diagnostic of Rickets. Rickets is caused by Vitamin D deficiency, which leads to defective mineralization of the growing bone matrix. Regarding the distractors, scurvy (Option B) presents with different X-ray features such as the "white line of Frankel," "Pelkan spurs," and "Wimberger’s ring" of the epiphysis, typically without the wide cupped metaphysis. While hypophosphatemia (Option C) can cause rickets-like bone changes, it is a metabolic cause and is less common than nutritional Vitamin D deficiency in India. The absence of "none" (Option D) is confirmed by the presence of these definitive signs. Thus, the specific "frayed and cupped" appearance of the radius and ulna on the X-ray confirms Rickets
questions.learning: The clinical finding of bow legs (genu varum) combined with the classic radiological findings of metaphyseal fraying, cupping, and splaying at the wrist is diagnostic of Rickets.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Following the recovery of a beheaded skull bone by the police, the relatives of a missing person want to confirm his identity. Which of the following techniques can be used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superimposition

The technique used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person is superimposition.

The superimposition technique is applied to the skull to determine whether it belongs to the person in the photograph. The following points can be used for comparisons such as the eyes, nasion, prosthion, zygomas, lower border of the nose, supraorbital ridges, lower border of the zygomas, angle of the jaw, external auditory meatus, teeth and the lower border of the upper jaw.

Other options:

Option B: Anthropometry is based on the principle that the skeletal dimensions do not change after the age of 21 years and the variation in the size of the different parts to one another. Descriptive data such as the color of the hair, eyes, complexion, and body marks are recorded. Body measurements are estimated such as height, anteroposterior diameter of head and trunk, the span of outstretched arms, the length of the left middle finger, left little finger, left forearm, left foot, length, and breadth of right ear, and color of left iris from the photographs.

Option C: DNA fingerprinting for forensic analysis is done to detect DNA from small amounts of samples from the crime scene. DNA fingerprinting uses restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLPs) or Polymerase chain reaction(PCR) to identify a person's unique pattern of DNA.

Option D: Cheiloscopy is also known as lip printing. Here, the fissures and grooves on the lip characteristic of a person are examined.
